articles.title: Former Marineland beluga whale dies at California theme park
articles.summary: A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.

image.caption: The entrance to SeaWorld is shown in Orlando, Fla., in January 2017. The theme park says a beluga whale that was relocated from Marineland in Ontario has died at its San Diego location. (John Raoux/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.
SeaWorld San Diego says ultrasound of 9-year-old male found intestinal issues

SeaWorld San Diego said in a Facebook post that Cyprus, a nine-year-old male beluga that arrived at the park on Aug. 22, stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound later determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.
It said Cyprus had been doing well since his arrival, eating consistently and interacting with his trainers and animal care team, along with two other rescued belugas.
But it said belugas can mask discomfort or underlying concerns that are not immediately visible, adding that a full necropsy will be conducted.

Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada, and 30 of its belugas and four dolphins were transferred to other facilities in a mass relocation effort.
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
SeaWorld San Diego said the other rescued belugas in its care are in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings.

"As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues," the facility said in its social media post on Sunday.
It said that after the necropsy is completed, the cause of Cyprus's death will be shared with the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

items: Everyone loved Marineland — then the tide turned. A look inside the park's final days

blocks.text: Less than two weeks ago, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago said Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga that was relocated from Marineland, died despite efforts to save her. Caspian had not been eating properly, and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels, Shedd said.
The aquarium said it performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo also died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

articles.title: El Niño-powered drought leaves Indonesian palm farmers high and dry as river recedes
articles.summary: Farmers are struggling financially, with some unable to sell their fruit and resorting to drastic measures like cutting fertilizer use by up to 70% to save costs, while others seek alternative income…

blocks.text: SANGGAU, Indonesia – Supendi, a 33-year-old palm fruit farmer, cooled his heels at a mill in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan for four frustrating days earlier this month trying to unload his harvest of fresh fruit bunches before being told to leave as the site was full.

For several weeks, local palm oil mills have cut their fresh fruit bunch purchases because storage tanks are filled with processed oil they cannot ship out as a prolonged drought driven by “super El Niño” conditions has dried out the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River.
“The fruit was not accepted,” Supendi told Reuters by telephone. “Now we’re at a loss as to how to sell it.”

He had driven from his hometown to the Multi Prima Entakai palm oil mill in the city of Sanggau in early October carrying 7 metric tons of fruit bunches from his small farm and neighbouring ones. He is one of thousands of smallholder farmers in West Kalimantan stuck with rotting fruit.
Supendi’s struggles illustrate one of the many impacts of this year’s extreme El Niño in Indonesia and Southeast Asia.

The weather phenomenon caused by a warming of the Pacific Ocean waters off South America typically causes hot, dry weather in Southeast Asia. But the strength of the current pattern has parched rivers and wells in Indonesia and fanned forest fires in Borneo — where West Kalimantan is located — and Sumatra that have spread choking haze over the province and as far as Malaysia and Singapore.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: How El Niño could impact the world’s weather in 2026-2027

blocks.text: West Kalimantan accounts for about 11% of palm oil output in Indonesia, the world’s largest producer, and analysts estimate fourth-quarter output across Indonesian Borneo could fall by 12% to 15% because of the El Niño-related disruptions.

The Kapuas — Indonesia’s longest river at 1,143 km — transports 40% of West Kalimantan’s palm oil output, according to data from the Indonesian Palm Oil Association, known as GAPKI. Sandbanks have emerged from the receding waters of the river, causing several barges and tugboats to run aground, according to Reuters witnesses.
Road delivery is a limited alternative, because trucks carry less than barges and fewer are available, millers say.

During El Niños in 2015 and 2018, similar droughts lasted for about a month, several local farmers said. But this year the Kapuas has dropped to a lower level and the effects have lasted for two months already.

Indonesia’s weather agency expects the start of the rainy season to be pushed back to November, from October normally, delaying the river’s resurgence and relief from the country’s most intense wildfires in 11 years.

Thirteen palm oil mills out of 50 in West Kalimantan have been affected by the transportation disruptions, accounting for roughly half of the province’s processing capacity, said Aris Supratman, who heads GAPKI’s West Kalimantan office.
He estimated palm oil supply from the province would fall by about 11% in September from August due to the backup.
“Because of the disruption, shipments are being delayed, and once their storage tanks are full, they inevitably have to limit production,” he said.
GAPKI has revised down its 2026 national palm oil production forecast by 2.9% as the dry weather slows fruit maturity.

Dian Kurniawan, 44, a manager at the Multi Prima Entakai mill that turned Supendi away, said the company’s fruit bunch purchases had dropped to 10,000 tons in September compared to the 30,000 tons it processed in July.
As of October 1, the mill held 8,200 tons of crude palm oil, near its storage tank capacity of 8,500 tons.

“We usually can deliver 2,000 tons in four days, but with trucks sometimes we can only deliver 100 tons per day,” Dian said, adding that truck shipments are not only slower than by barge but also three times the cost.

Farmers unable to sell their harvests face difficulties maintaining their palm trees, said Indra Rustandi, who heads the West Kalimantan branch of smallholder farmers group APKASINDO, adding the lack of income has caused some to cut their fertilizer applications by up to 70% to save costs.

Another Sanggau smallholder, 63-year-old Rahmat Wiyono, said he struggled to sell his fruit over the last two months, sometimes driving six hours only to be offered 2,650 rupiah ($0.15) per kg of fruit bunches, compared with three hours to his regular mill, which had paid 3,400 rupiah.

“Some of our friends haven’t had any harvest for the past two months, so they have had to find other ways to supplement their daily income,” such as selling homemade cakes and donuts, he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Limited evidence’ of protester violence at Sydney demonstration against Israeli president Isaac Herzog visit
articles.summary:
Amid police brutality allegations, Law Enforcement Conduct Commission inquiry hears protesters ‘largely peaceful’

  • Get our

blocks.text: An inquiry into a Sydney rally against the Israeli president’s visit has so far found protesters were “largely peaceful” and there is “limited evidence of physical violence on the part of the protesters”.

The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) kicked off its inquiry into the February protest at Sydney’s town hall against the visit of Isaac Herzog on Monday, outlining a number of issues it is examining, including police use of OC spray and “police boasting about gratuitous force”.

Lecc launched its investigation after widespread allegations of police brutality at the protest. Viral video footage showed police punching multiple protesters, and grabbing Muslim worshippers while they undertook sunset prayers.

Monday’s opening address was heard in public before closing for five-week long private examinations. The watchdog agreed to hold a portion of the hearing in private after the NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, made a last-minute bid to have the entire hearings held in private, delaying the scheduled hearing by almost a month.

Counsel assisting the Lecc, Kirsten Edwards SC, said in her opening address that the evidence is far from concluded. But so far it shows: “there is limited evidence of physical violence on the part of the protesters. The protest appears to have been largely peaceful in its early stages.”
“Later conduct by protesters, described in the evidence of police as aggressive, was for the most part verbal and connected to a desire to march,” Edwards said.
“Footage also shows protest organisers at various points apparently attempting to defuse conflict with police.”

Police charged 30 people in the months after the protest with various offences, including hinder arrest and assault police. But almost a dozen of those protesters have had the charges against them withdrawn.
Edwards said that the Lecc would examine police conduct according to a law in place at the time, which restricted protesters’ ability to march.
This law, known as the Public Assembly Restriction Declaration, or Pard, was found unconstitutional by the state’s highest court two months after the protest.
On Friday before the Downing centre local court, police withdrew charges against seven people, after four people had theirs withdrawn in recent months.

blocks.caption: New South Wales police commissioner Mal Lanyon. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP

blocks.text: In June, the local court set a joint hearing date for 25 of the approximately 30 people initially charged, which is expected to last six weeks in the local court in July 2027. After the dropped charges, the number of people part of that joint hearing is now down to 17.

Edwards said Lecc was examining multiple widespread concerns that had emerged in the 400 complaints lodged by the public and the 1,000 hours of footage the Lecc has reviewed. She said this included the use of OC spray against the mobility impaired and in close proximity to people’s faces.

She said Lecc was also examining “frequent pushing and shoving of protesters during crowd dispersal … police moving at speed and in formation towards fleeing protesters … The use of force during arrests and, finally, some police boasting about gratuitous force”.
“It also includes the allegation that protesters were contained within an area from which they could not leave, sometimes described as kettling,” she said.
“There are also instances of officers showing care towards the elderly and vulnerable, and showing concern about members of the protest being close to hazards.”

Edwards said Lecc was examining the issues via a number of case studies, including a man in his 60s who was struck in the face, and the “prayer incident” where Muslim worshippers were dragged away by police.
Edwards said the commission was examining questions on whether the police’s conduct was endemic “or was in some way sanctioned or encouraged by senior officers on the night.”
The inquiry heard that a briefing was held with officers ahead of the protest, where senior officers including Lanyon spoke but no recordings or notes were made.
Edwards said a common recollection from people present at the briefing was that “officers were clearly told the protest was intended to remain static and that a march was not to be permitted”.
An opening address was also given on behalf of Lanyon by David Sulan SC. He said there was “an unprecedented level of serious verbal abuse that was directed towards police”.
“Despite these difficulties, there were many positive acts of policing before and during the protest,” he said.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] JAZA’s painful question: Why aren’t we winning?
articles.summary: The numbers explain why I found Jaime Zobel de Ayala's speech before the Makati Business Club more unsettling than inspirational

items: The Philippines risks being left behind in global investment due to fundamental issues in talent, infrastructure, energy, regulatory environment, and institutional stability, as highlighted by Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala.
Foreign direct investment in the Philippines has declined significantly, and while ASEAN countries are attracting capital, the Philippines must address its weaknesses to remain competitive.

The real competition lies not among local companies but between the Philippines and other countries, emphasizing the urgency for the government and businesses to collaborate on improving the country's foundational issues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Global capital is moving, but the Philippines risks being left behind. Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala’s warning on talent, infrastructure, energy, regulatory environment, and institutional stability exposes a harder truth: unless the country fixes the fundamentals, the next wave of factories, data centers, and supply-chain investments may simply go elsewhere.

There was one line in the speech delivered by Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala (JAZA) before the Makati Business Club (MBC) last Thursday, October 15, that should have made every policymaker in the room cringe.

As global companies diversify their supply chains, he said, Philippine businesses should stop worrying only about which company, industrial park, or industry captures the next investment. The more important question is whether the Philippines itself is winning.
I would take him literally.

JAZA effectively handed us a five-part due-diligence checklist for the country: talent, infrastructure, energy, regulatory environment, and institutional stability. These are precisely the factors a multinational corporation would examine before committing billions to a factory, semiconductor facility, data center, or regional headquarters.

blocks.caption: JAZA: Does the Philippines have what it takes to win big investments?

blocks.text: Let’s put his question to the numbers. Start with the outcome that ultimately matters: investment.

Foreign direct investment flowing into the Philippines fell 23.9% to US$4.071 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) report cited in Zobel’s speech.

At about the same time, a participant in the Jefferies-Regis Partners Philippines Conference reportedly observed that fewer foreign investors than expected had traveled to Manila. Neither statistic proves that investors are abandoning the country, but both give JAZA’s question greater urgency.

The uncomfortable part is that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) itself is not starved of investment. Supply chains are being rearranged, semiconductor ecosystems are expanding, data centers are multiplying, and global companies are still looking for places to deploy capital. The issue is not whether money is moving. It is whether enough of it is moving here.

Take talent, the first item on JAZA’s checklist. The Philippines has the demographic story investors like to hear: a young population and a large working-age labor force. But demographics are not the same as human capital.

In the latest Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), only 16% of Filipino 15-year-olds reached basic proficiency in mathematics, compared with 72% in Vietnam. That gap matters more because artificial intelligence raises the value of higher-order skills and threatens to automate many routine service jobs.

Infrastructure is less disastrous, but hardly a decisive advantage. In the latest Logistics Performance Index of the World Bank (WB), the Philippines scored 3.3, roughly level with Vietnam, ahead of Indonesia but below Malaysia and Thailand. That suggests that our logistics system is serviceable, but not strong enough to offset weaknesses elsewhere.

This is why JAZA’s warning about accountability matters. He said infrastructure must not merely be built. The right projects must be built well, with every project and peso fully accountable. A peso wasted on bad infrastructure produces two losses: taxpayers lose the money, and businesses fail to receive the roads, ports, and transport systems that could have improved competitiveness.
Then comes energy, where the disadvantage becomes much harder to ignore.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] JAZA’s painful question: Why aren’t we winning?

blocks.text: Using a common benchmark for large business users, Philippine electricity costs about US$0.153 per kWh in March 2026, versus $0.119 in Thailand, $0.116 in Malaysia, $0.081 in Vietnam and $0.062 in Indonesia. That puts Philippine power almost 89% above Vietnam’s and about 147% above Indonesia’s. (READ: Cheaper PH electricity? Go beyond system loss; fix costly power contracts)

A semiconductor plant or hyperscale data center does not care about the reasons electricity is expensive. It puts the number on a spreadsheet and calculates what operating here will cost over the next decade.

Regulation and institutional stability, meanwhile, are less about headline rankings than predictability. The Philippines sits roughly in the middle of its regional peers on formal regulatory quality measures, but capital does not price rules in isolation. It prices uncertainty — shifting policies, unpredictable permits, inconsistent interpretation of contracts, and institutions whose credibility changes with personalities.
That uncertainty carries a cost.
Investors can model wages, freight, and electricity. What they find much harder to model is whether the rules of the game will still look the same five or ten years from now.
Seen together, the numbers explain why I found Zobel’s speech more unsettling than inspirational.

The Philippines does not fail every test. Our logistics performance is respectable, and our regulatory environment is not uniquely worse than those of all our neighbors, which makes the situation more frustrating.
Where we are weak, the weaknesses are fundamental: the quality of future workers and the price of the electricity that future industries will consume.
These are not problems a tax incentive can permanently hide.

JAZA’s broader point was that Philippine conglomerates can continue competing fiercely for customers, employees, capital, and foreign partners, while recognizing that no single corporation can fix education, national infrastructure, energy policy, or institutional credibility.
That requires government and business to work on the foundations together.

And this is where JAZA’s deceptively simple question becomes uncomfortable. The Philippines has spent decades discussing expensive power, weak education, infrastructure gaps, regulatory friction, and governance. None of these problems is newly discovered.
The diagnosis has never really been our biggest problem.
Execution has.

That is also why his call for accountability deserves more attention than it received. Infrastructure spending does not make a country more competitive merely because billions appear in a national budget.

Education does not improve because classrooms are built. An energy policy does not become successful because a generating capacity is announced. Regulation does not become investment-friendly simply because agencies promise faster approvals.
What matters is whether these systems deliver results.

The Philippines still has advantages that many countries would gladly trade for: a young population, English-language capability, geographic proximity to major Asian supply chains, a long-established electronics sector, and access to a rapidly growing ASEAN market.
But potential has an expiration date.

Supply chains being redesigned today will not wait indefinitely for us to fix electricity prices. Semiconductor investments awarded elsewhere do not create supplier networks here. Data centers built in neighboring markets create ecosystems there. Workers displaced by artificial intelligence cannot simply wait for an education system to catch up ten years from now. (READ: Building a ‘Silicon Valley in Tarlac’? Manny Pangilinan wants in.)
Capital moves before governments are ready.
Consequently, we may have been focusing on the wrong competition.
The real contest is not Ayala versus Aboitiz, one industrial estate against another, or one Philippine company trying to land the next multinational investor.
The real contest is between the Philippines and everyone else.
And global capital is already voting. – Rappler.com

articles.title: France counts the cost of worst unrest in years; Macron urges calm
articles.summary: Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country

blocks.text: ON FIRE. A person raises an arm during civil unrest, the day after a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 18, 2026.
Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country

items: French President Emmanuel Macron called for calm after widespread unrest and riots across France, resulting in thousands of arrests and significant property damage.
Protests erupted over high living costs and declining public services, with Macron acknowledging the legitimate grievances of peaceful protesters while condemning the violence from fringe groups.
The unrest led to clashes with police, injuries among officers, and extensive damage to businesses, prompting government discussions on measures to prevent further violence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PARIS, France – French President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday, October 18, a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services.
Fresh clashes broke out in Paris and Marseille, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses.
Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across France.

blocks.caption: PROTEST. Residents gather during a protest following a fire at the town hall in Limoges, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters

blocks.text: “Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
“Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”
Saturday’s unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt.
Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate grievances and their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc.

He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, as demanded by some right-wing politicians, but said the government would act to allow prefects to ban protests if necessary to protect public buildings and local businesses.
The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting.

One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris. Police made 2,400 arrests across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.

blocks.caption: UNREST. Riot police operate during civil unrest, the day after a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters

blocks.text: Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and protesters had set fire to piles of bicycles. A Reuters witness said there appeared to be several hundred protesters in the area.

A massive clean-up operation took place in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and from Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.
“It’s like a war zone here!” exclaimed Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children and said the unrest forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique.

More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.

While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.

Far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner going into next year’s presidential campaign, also called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused and ransacked.
“Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France,” she said in a video address.

blocks.caption: CALL FOR CALM. French President Emmanuel Macron appears on screen as he makes a television address to the nation a day after clashes during a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, near Marseille, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters

blocks.text: Hard-left France Unbowed presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students.

In Limoges, famed for its porcelain, the collapse of the town hall’s clock tower in a fiery blaze revived memories of the 2019 fire that devastated Paris’ Notre Dame cathedral. Mayor Guillaume Guerin said not enough officers from the national police had been deployed to his city.

“There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives,” Guerin told Reuters on Sunday. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall.

Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. “Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” Lescure said in a statement.

French retailer Carrefour’s CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company’s shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the tens of millions of euros. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo overtakes Padilla in Octa’s 2028 Senate survey
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Raffy Tulfo topped the list of potential senatorial candidates for the 2028 elections, overtaking fellow Sen. Robin Padilla, according to the latest survey by Octa…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Raffy Tulfo topped the list of potential senatorial candidates for the 2028 elections, overtaking fellow Sen. Robin Padilla, according to the latest survey by Octa Research.

In its non-commissioned “Tugon ng Masa” survey conducted from September 28 to October 4, 2026, the respondents were presented with a hypothetical list of potential senatorial candidates and were asked: “I have here a list of names that may run in the May 2028 elections. If the May 2028 elections will be held today, who will you likely vote for as SENATOR? You may choose up to 12 names.”

The results showed that Tulfo obtained the highest voting preference at 47 percent, followed by Padilla (45 percent), Cayetano (44 percent), and Sotto (42 percent). Octa Research noted that “the four share a rank range of first to fourth, indicating that their relative order cannot be treated as statistically fixed.”
Octa said the four candidates’ ranking ranges overlapped, meaning their relative positions could not be considered statistically fixed.

Other hypothetical senatorial bets who made it in the “Magic 12” are former Senator Grace Poe (36 percent), Senator Loren Legarda (31 percent), with rank ranging from fifth to sixth and fifth to ninth, respectively.

They are followed by Makati City Mayor and former Senator Abby Binay (29 percent), Mark Lapid (28 percent), Senator Francis Escudero (27 percent), Education Secretary Sonny Angara and Manny Pacquiao each at 25 percent, Ben Tulfo (23 percent), and Senator Jinggoy Estrada (22 percent). The polling firm said that they remain in the preliminary top 12 amid their overlapping rank ranges.

The survey also included former Senator Koko Pimentel and Salvador Panelo (both at 20 percent), Senator Mark Villar (19 percent), and Gringo Honasan and Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino (both at 18 percent) in the broad statistical range vying for the last available slots.
Octa Research also pointed out that Raffy took over Padilla’s slot as the hypothetical top senatorial bet from the second quarter survey held from July 4-11, 2026.
Padilla previously led the survey with 53.9 percent voting preference, followed by Raffy with 47.4 percent.

The polling firm also shared that some names were removed from the survey list upon their request, while some individuals who received less than 1 percent of vote were omitted from the published results.
Octa cautioned that the results reflect voter preferences during the survey period and should not be interpreted as a forecast of the 2028 elections.
The survey included face-to-face interviews among 1,200 adult respondents with ±3 percentage-point margin of error at the 95 percent confidence level./dp

articles.title: Kylie Minogue songs already used to train AI as tech firms ‘strong-arm’ Australian government, music body warns
articles.summary:
Of the dozens of countries approached to water down their laws, Australia appears to be the only one considering it, publishers’ group says

  • Get our

blocks.text: AI has already been trained on the works of Australian artists including Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave without compensation, the peak global body for music rights has claimed, as the Australian government has been warned against giving in to “strong-arming” from tech companies seeking to weaken copyright law.

The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) – which represents Sony, Warner and Universal as well as thousands of independent publishers on six continents – has warned that of the dozens of countries approached to water down copyright laws, Australia appears to be the only to consider doing so.
John Phelan, the ICMP’s managing director, told Guardian Australia AI companies were asking policymakers to “legitimise larceny”.
“They’re trying to strong-arm Australian policymakers into ‘if you don’t do this, we won’t invest’.”
In July, Anthony Albanese said it would be “theft” if artists did not retain control over whether their work was used to build and train AI, and what they were paid for its use.

Music, film, media and news organisations had expressed concerns the government was being lobbied by global tech companies behind closed doors to weaken Australia’s copyright laws to help train AI models, without compensating the creative sectors.
But government and opposition members of a parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence appeared to revisit the issue this week, describing the current situation as a stalemate.

They said AI models were already training on copyrighted works in the United States without compensating creators – but that without changes to local copyright laws, those companies were withholding training frontier AI models in Australia.

In a joint letter to the prime minister this week, the inquiry’s Labor chair, Jo Briskey, and its deputy chair, Liberal senator Jonathon Duniam, recommended the government “examine current copyright settings” while ensuring creators retain control and are paid.

The independent senator David Pocock has raised concerns that the committee was coming to a position on copyright predetermined by the prime minister, after staffer edits were seen in the letter. Briskey has rejected the claim.
AI companies’ demands

The ICMP has been tracking how AI companies are attempting to change copyright law in different jurisdictions to allow training. Phelan highlighted methods that the companies had used to train their models on music, such as with spreadsheets containing millions of lines of music available on YouTube.

A key claim of the AI industry is that its models are not trained on Australian content due to copyright rules. However, in evidence provided exclusively to Guardian Australia, ICMP showed Google’s Gemini was able to reproduce lyrics from Australian artists including Kylie Minogue, G-Flip and Nick Cave.
Phelan also pointed to an AI training dataset reported by the Atlantic in June, which contains more than 12m songs pulled from YouTube videos, including tracks from Minogue, Cave and Hilltop Hoods.
Google was approached for comment.
Phelan said 62 countries had considered making their own legal changes but none of the others had bought into AI companies’ demands.
after newsletter promotion

“There isn’t a single country among the other 61 [countries] … which has introduced a new text and data mining exception for commercial purposes, or reduce the idea of exclusive rights and copyright,” Phelan said.
“The world is very much watching what Australia does.”

“It’s fair to say the global music industry, as well as all creative industries worldwide we work with, are appalled by the idea of a statutory scheme or a government deal which would interfere with how Australian industries work and contract around the world.”

Anthropic’s special envoy, Jeffrey Bleich, told the AI committee last week the company was not trying to dictate terms, but had shared information with the Australian government about training and what the implications would be “with respect to our capacity to operate here”.
“You can’t license the entire internet. Billions and billions of information exists there which is available to be viewed and studied, and that’s essentially what training is,” he said.
“Under existing Australian law, it’s our understanding that that could be determined to be illegal if we weren’t able to find a licence with every single person who had rights within Australia.”

OpenAI’s chief of economic policy, Adam Cohen, said the fair use exception in US law “fundamentally protects” the development of new technology. He pointed to agreements made with News Corp and the Guardian as examples of where the company makes deals for the use of work, despite arguing US law did not require such.

Phelan said he believed panic had set in among the AI companies over the sheer cost of investment and the need to make a return, coupled with the ongoing litigation over copyright in the US. He said they may be looking to Australia for a legislative solution.
“They’re seeing the legislative side as being the way to try to [find] a place to do business without licences, which will secure their future business model.”

In a submission to the inquiry, Guardian Australia said that undermining copyright protection would have a “profound impact on civil society” and copyright-protected material should only be available for AI training with the rights holder’s explicit prior authorisation.

articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waivers, accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump again accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. The remarks come amid renewed tensions over US policy toward Moscow including waiving…

image.caption: Trump (right) repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the US midterm election [FILE: September 22, 2026]Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trumpon Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.

"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.
Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.
He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms
Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February.
Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices.
Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election.
How Trump is helping Putin
The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow.
"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy."
He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days.
Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "We are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies.
Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism

Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg.

After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths.
Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.

blocks.text: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

items: If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

blocks.text: Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
Foma has the same rule for his operatives.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.
"Putin won't live forever," he said.

articles.title: Outrage after Meta suspends No Kings Instagram account during protests
articles.summary:
‘Meta owes us an explanation,’ group says as organizers fear censorship after account goes dark for several hours

The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have…

blocks.text: The coalition leaders behind nationwide pro-democracy protests that have drawn millions of Americans to the streets in recent years were frustrated when its Instagram account was temporarily shut down during its latest demonstration on Saturday.
The No Kings movement’s account went dark for several hours while protests focused on increasing early voter turnout were underway, sparking censorship fears.
Meta apologized on Saturday and blamed the account’s temporary suspension on an automated action that’s triggered “when accounts post, share or comment at very high frequencies”.
“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,” Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, wrote on X. “Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize.”

“We have regained access to our accounts, but Meta still owes us an explanation,” the No Kings Coalition posted on their Instagram page, on Sunday. “Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”
In a longer statement, Stone cited the “high volume” of reading profiles, posts and hashtags in “intense bursts” on Saturday caused their AI tool to detect the activity as automated bot traffic.

“This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. An automated re-review of the removal action an hour later recognized that shouldn’t have happened and restored the account,” Stone said. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account. We want to reiterate our sincere apology for the error.”
Organizers remained skeptical about Meta’s explanation that high-frequency posting triggered an automated response, and said members “posted only a handful of times and livestreamed to thousands”.
Senator Bernie Sanders also expressed concerns on Sunday, on X, saying that “billionaire ownership of the media” had resulted in the suspension of the No Kings account.

Connecticut senator Chris Murphy called for an investigation into the incident in his own social media post, saying it was an indictment of Meta’s “outsized influence” on US culture and politics. “How were they not ready for the biggest day of anti-Trump protest of the campaign?” Murphy said. “An investigation is warranted, at the very least, to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump.”

Despite the technical blip, hundreds of planned events continued. At the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats, many of whom were dancing and held signs saying “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!”
In Atlanta, city councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd: “The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?”

On the streets of downtown Los Angeles, protesters carried umbrellas to protect them from the sweltering heat and a band trailed behind them on a rolling stage, the New York Times reported; the crowds cheered calls for abolishing ICE and passing California’s billionaire tax.

The No Kings movement began last summer, in response to a broad set of concerns about federal layoffs, immigration enforcement and foreign wars. The demonstrations have continued to tackle a wide range of issues, and typically lean into anti-Trump fervor.

This year’s focus on voting ahead of the midterm elections is in part due to the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, as well as fears about Trump once again sowing chaos by baselessly calling election results into question.

No Kings organizers said they planned to recruit volunteers at Saturday’s events to mobilize in case of “election sabotage”, Leah Greenberg, a co-executive director of Indivisible, a progressive group that helps organize No Kings events, previously told the Guardian.

articles.title: Obama condemns comments by ‘border czar’ that Ilhan Omar could ‘of course’ be denaturalized
articles.summary:
Ex-president urges Americans to defend congresswoman, saying ‘there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her’

Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s…
articles.byline: José Olivares and Sanya Mansoor in New York

blocks.text: Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her.
Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.”

He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs, adding: “if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her – or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.” Obama, too, has had his citizenship scrutinized by Trump, who more than a decade ago fueled false conspiracy theories that Obama was born in Kenya and therefore not eligible to be president.
Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, was asked on Saturday by a Fox News host whether the investigation into Omar could involve “denaturalizing and then deporting her”, Homan answered: “Of course”.
“If you lie during the naturalization process, there is a process to denaturalize somebody,” Homan said. “We’ve done it before. It’s a long, tedious process, but it’s been done before.
“And certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen.”

Homan’s comments were the first remarks explicitly mentioning denaturalization and deportation in connection with Omar that were attributed by name to a top Trump administration official since federal agents raided the Minnesota US House representative’s home on 12 October.

The search of Omar’s home sparked major backlash and accusations that the Trump administration was weaponizing the federal government to target a political rival whom the president and his supporters have openly fantasized about denaturalizing and deporting.

The federal government’s investigation into the most prominent Somali American in the US is to see whether Omar or her family violated any laws when obtaining her citizenship. The investigation was launched only weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Homan also seemed to imply during his Fox News appearance that the federal government is investigating Omar for other allegations – but refused to give details.
“I’m not going to go there,” Homan said. “I know things, but that’s a question for the FBI.”

Omar – a naturalized US citizen from Somalia – was a child when her father filled out the immigration paperwork which the federal government is evidently scrutinizing. Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, died in June 2020.

blocks.caption: Tom Homan applauds as Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Syracuse, New York, on 9 October.  Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Obama stated in his post on X that Omar arrived in the US with her father when she was 12, and five years later, when her father became a naturalized citizen, she became one, too, because she was 17. (An 18-year-old would have had to apply for citizenship separately, he noted.)

“Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen,” he wrote. “Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone – all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.”
In a letter after her home was searched, Omar’s attorneys accused the US justice department of potentially influencing an election in violation of longstanding internal policy.

The move to investigate Omar came amid a heightened offensive by the administration in pursuit of its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. In addition to funneling resources and deploying droves of officials to arrest, detain and deport undocumented immigrants throughout the country, the administration has also escalated its on offensive on legal migration.
The administration has been pursuing dozens of cases nationwide in which they are attempting to denaturalize Americans born outside of the US, who they claim fraudulently obtained their citizenship.
As Homan alluded to on Sunday, the lengthy denaturalization process requires a federal investigation and drawn-out court proceedings.
after newsletter promotion
Nonetheless, as of April, the US justice department had reportedly identified nearly 400 foreign-born citizens that it sought to investigate.

The investigation into Omar follows unsubstantiated accusations by rightwing figures who support Trump that she obtained her citizenship fraudulently. Omar denies the accusations, which also include allegations that her ex-husband is her brother, whom she only married so he could obtain immigration status in the US.
The federal government reportedly seized Omar’s phone during the raid on her home and has issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including of Omar’s relatives.
Omar’s attorneys have demanded that the federal government return her property and preserve any audio or video taken during the search.

Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was eight and spent years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She and her family came to the US in the 1990s, and she became a naturalized US citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
There is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”, said her attorneys’ letter, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Even veterans at the Department of Justice expressed shock over the targeting of Omar, according to reporting by NBC News. “I was astounded to see a search of a sitting congressperson this close to an election,” said Peter Carr, a former career justice department spokesperson, NBC News reported.

“Historically, the department has been very adamant that politics plays no role in investigative decisions they make and they try very hard to avoid taking overt actions that might even have the perception of influencing an election.”
After the raid on her home, Omar posted on X that she was “ok”.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar also wrote. She said: “Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns” for years – and “this is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
“I will not be silenced,” Omar added.

articles.title: Ombudsman dismisses Urdaneta mayor, 7 others for defying suspension order
articles.summary: The penalties include the cancellation of civil service eligibility, permanent disqualification from public office, a ban on taking civil service exams, and forfeiture of retirement benefits

blocks.text: DISMISSED. The Office of the Ombudsman orders the dismissal of Urdaneta Mayor Julio 'Rammy'Parayno III and several other local officials.
The penalties include the cancellation of civil service eligibility, permanent disqualification from public office, a ban on taking civil service exams, and forfeiture of retirement benefits

items: The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the dismissal of Urdaneta City Mayor Julio Parayno III, Vice Mayor Jimmy Parayno, and six city councilors for grave misconduct and gross neglect of duty related to their handling of a suspension order.

The Paraynos continued to perform their official duties despite a 12-month suspension imposed by the Office of the President, while the councilors refused to assume their designated posts during the suspension.

Penalties include cancellation of civil service eligibility, disqualification from public office, and forfeiture of retirement benefits, although other charges against the Paraynos were dismissed due to insufficient evidence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PANGASINAN, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the dismissal of Urdaneta City Mayor Julio “Rammy” Parayno III, Vice Mayor Jimmy Parayno, and six city councilors for defying a Malacañang suspension order against the city’s top two officials.

In a consolidated decision dated April 15, the Ombudsman found the Paraynos guilty of grave misconduct for continuing to perform their duties despite a 12-month suspension ordered by the Office of the President in January 2025.
The six councilors were found liable for gross neglect of duty for refusing to assume the posts assigned to them by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).
The penalties include cancellation of civil service eligibility, perpetual disqualification from public office, a ban on taking civil service examinations, and forfeiture of retirement benefits.

The case stemmed from a complaint filed by a barangay chairman, Michael Brian Perez, in October 2022. He was placed under indefinite suspension that June, after a manifesto sought his removal as president of the Liga ng mga Barangay (LnB), a post that automatically made him an ex-officio nenver of the city council.
Perez alleged the national LnB and the DILG both backed him, and that the DILG found no legal basis for his suspension.

On January 3, 2025, Malacañang found the Paraynos liable for grave misconduct and grave abuse of authority and ordered their suspension for six months each, or a total of 12 months. It then directed the DILG to implement the order.

But when DILG personnel attempted to serve the suspension documents on January 7, the mayor’s staff refused to receive them, while the vice mayor’s office was locked and chained. This prompted the DILG to post copies of the order on the office doors.
The Paraynos subsequently argued that they had not been personally served and questioned the enforcement of the suspension order during that year’s election period.
The Ombudsman, however, cited a subsequent court ruling that upheld the posting of the documents as constructive service.

The decision also cited Mayor Parayno’s continued exercise of official functions, including signing disbursement vouchers, issuing a business permit, and attending a flag-raising ceremony with the vice mayor.
The Ombudsman rejected the officials’ claim of good faith, finding that their refusal to receive the orders and continued performance of their duties constituted intentional wrongdoing.
The Paraynos stepped aside on March 31, 2025, after the DILG designated councilors Rio Virgilio Esteves and Blesildo Sumera as acting mayor and vice mayor.
Both Paraynos were reelected in May 2025.
Six councilors were found liable for refusing DILG orders designating them to temporarily replace the suspended officials.
The DILG initially designated Franco Paolo Del Prado and Warren Andrada, followed by Aurelio Agsalud and Franklin Villanueva.

The orders were later issued to Jhan Hero Sumera and Alfonso Miguel Del Prado, who formally declined the appointments in a joint letter dated March 25, 2025, arguing that there were no vacancies to fill.
The Ombudsman found that the councilors deliberately avoided receiving the designation orders and rejected their argument that the case had become moot because city hall operations continued.
Under the Local Government Code, the highest-ranking members of the city council assume the responsibilities of a mayor or vice mayor during a suspension.

The Ombudsman dismissed other charges against the Paraynos, including grave abuse of authority, conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, conduct unbecoming of a public official, and disgraceful and immoral conduct, citing insufficient evidence.

The copy of the decision reviewed bears a certification stamp dated September 28, 2026, and a receiving stamp dated October 13, 2026. It remains unclear whether any of the respondents have appealed or sought reconsideration. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Times’s investigation adds more intrigue to infamous OJ Simpson case
articles.summary:
Report reveals that a shady mobser-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up murder

An in-depth investigation by the

blocks.text: An in-depth investigation by the New York Times is raising further questions about the high-profile OJ Simpson case, in which the former football player was accused in the 1990s of killing his ex-wife – and whether a shady mobster-turned-informant may have been involved in helping cover up the murder.

The Times’s investigation revealed that California prosecutors were unable to fully investigate whether Simpson, who was accused but not convicted of his ex-wife’s murder, may have had an accomplice at the scene of the crime.

The extensive journalistic investigation, based on previously sealed court records and interviews, adds further intrigue to the infamous Simpson case. No one was ever criminally convicted for the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

That year, Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were found stabbed to death outside her home in Los Angeles. The American professional football player and actor, OJ Simpson, was suspected in the murder. Simpson’s prosecution gained international attention and became a media spectacle, being deemed the “trial of the century”.

Simpson was acquitted by a jury in 1995 after a lengthy trial. The Los Angeles police department, which investigated the case, had a long history of racism. Simpson’s attorneys pointed to the racist policing practices and the department’s handling of key evidence, helping them secure the acquittal. Simpson was later held liable for the deaths by a jury in a civil case.

But the New York Times has now revealed that a shady informant began revealing information about Simpson’s case towards the end of the prosecution. The informant, a wealthy mobster named Joseph Ippolito, had become a snitch after spending years on the run from the federal government.
The information Ippolito had may have been key to the trial, but it was far too late for the prosecution to include his testimony.

Ippolito, a longtime drug runner throughout the US known as Joey, came from the New Jersey underworld, where his father was a player within the DeCavalcante crime family, a major Italian American criminal organization. After a stint in prison for trafficking drugs in the east coast, he moved to California in the late 1980s and managed an Italian restaurant.

There, he was able to embed himself in the inner circles of the Los Angeles elite. Ippolito befriended Al Cowlings, a former football star and close friend of OJ Simpson. But while he spent time with Los Angeles celebrities, Ippolito continued selling and trafficking drugs.

In 1992, he was arrested by authorities again in a sting operation. But in May 1994, eight months after his sentencing, Ippolito escaped from his Florida prison. His brother helped him arrive back in Los Angeles, where he remained in hiding as a wanted fugitive.

That year, the murder of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman took place in Los Angeles. When authorities attempted to arrest OJ Simpson, he fled. His friend Cowlings, the former football player, led the police on a widely-publicized chase through Los Angeles with Simpson in the car.

After Simpson’s arrest, officials found Ippolito’s information in Cowlings’ wallet, leading them to urgently search for the mobster-at-large. Eventually they found Ippolito and arrested him. But he decided to flip and become an informant for the US government.

As an informant, Ippolito revealed information about various drug deals throughout the country and helped federal agencies set up sting operations. But Ippolito also reportedly shared information with the government about the Los Angeles murders.
The New York Times raises three separate theories for Ippolito’s involvement in the Simpson case, which he was seemingly willing to share with authorities:
1) In one version, Ippolito told federal prosecutors he had information he learned from Cowlings about the murders, including the supposed location of the missing weapon.
2) In another version, Ippolito’s brother told a reporter with the Times that Ippolito may have been at the scene of the killings. The brother said Ippolito literally had blood on his hands.
3) And in a third version, Ippolito was prepared to help Simpson escape during the wild police chase throughout Los Angeles.

“Taken together, the material points in different directions but veers significantly from the official account that has been proffered by the police and prosecutors,” the New York Times reports. “With many of the key players now dead, it’s possible the full truth will never be known.”

Ippolito’s brother, who told the Times he had seen his brother’s hands with blood on them, later asked the publication for money and then recanted his statement to the publication. According to the report, the brother said he had been “offered a ton of money” to share his story elsewhere, likely a television program.
The extent of Ippolito’s involvement is not fully known. Authorities interviewed by the Times expressed doubts on how involved Ippolito was and the value of his information in the case.

articles.title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
articles.summary: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies says the country has been "bundled together" in measures aimed at curbing cheap imports.

blocks.text: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".
He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.
The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.
It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.

There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.
Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures.
"Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia.
"Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help.
"I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."
The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.
The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years".
"Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.

Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.
But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.
All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".
At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.
Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.
Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids.
"The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks."
"Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."
Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history".
"We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."
