articles.title: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says US President Donald Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

blocks.text: TRUMP AND PUTIN. File photo shows US President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin during the G20 leaders summit in Buenos Aires, Argentina on November 30, 2018.
Marcos Brindicci/REUTERS
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says US President Donald Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

items: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia, claiming it will embolden Moscow to continue its aggression against Ukraine.

Trump's executive order, which waives key sanctions and tariffs related to Russia, is seen as undermining efforts to pressure Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, with Zelenskyy warning it could lead to increased Russian attacks.
The waiver has received mixed reactions, with some US politicians expressing concern over its implications for US-Russia relations and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON DC, USA – US President Donald Trump‘s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday, October 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”

An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night, October 16, waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US

The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelenskyy said Trump’s latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday. “This certainly does not stop the war.”
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment,” posting on X on Friday that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.

Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Saturday, she did not directly criticize Trump for waiving sanctions, but she said she would not have made that choice.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law” while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.

But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday’s executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate.”
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.

“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy.
But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday’s waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month, the Ukrainian leader predicted.

“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey … It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: For chefs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze, success is on the menu — but so is learning
articles.summary: Food entrepreneurs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze head back to the classroom, proving that even successful chefs still have more to learn

blocks.text: Bolinao, Pangasinan wakes to the sounds of water.

Before the first guest opens the door at Birdland Beach Club, the sea has already been at work all day, dragging itself up the sand and letting go over and over, the slow percussion of a shore town that has never known silence.

By the time the sun clears the treeline, the roast smell from the coffee bar is pushing its way out the open windows, warm and nutty, drifting across the lot where Joanna Ledesma’s Kopi Kubo Kollective stands on the highway: a coffee shop built on land with a rice field view, where the evening fog lifts.
Two hundred kilometers south, in a small dining room on D. Tuazon, Santa Mesa Heights in Quezon City, a different pot has been at work since morning.
At Nam Jai Thai Noodle House, khao soi is a study in contrast: soft egg-wheat noodles below, crisp ones on top, all meeting in coconut-curry broth.
The broth takes six to eight hours to prepare. Jeremaine Sze makes the curry paste from scratch, imports ingredients from Thailand, and works with local farms to source herbs and spices.
Just like in most things she does, there is no shortcut: no pressure cooker and no premade paste.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze with her staff  at Nam Jai Thai Noodle House. Contributed photo

blocks.text: Two women head these two kitchens. Ledesma owns the Birdland Beach Club and runs the Kopi Kubo Kollective in Bolinao, while Sze leads as the executive chef and owner of Nam Jai in Quezon City
The businesses are different. But the question that brought the two owners to the same culinary school was the same.
Although both have long been passionate about cooking, they always get the the question: “Are you a culinary graduate?”
Ledesma heard it while running a restaurant and coffee shop in Malaysia.
“Everybody’s telling me, ‘Are you a culinary graduate?’…I felt like there’s something missing on my side,” she recalled.
Ledesma knew how to cook and create menus, but the question left her feeling inadequate.
Working with a staff who had formal culinary training also brought the knowledge gap into focus.
For Ledesma, the hardest part was memorization — the terminologies refusing to stick to a 40-year-old brain.
She recalled hearing terms such as “mise en place” and “bouquet garni” and realizing she could not explain them, even as the head of the kitchen.

blocks.caption: Joanna Ledesma prepares meals for 50 people in her resort. Contributed photo
Joanna Ledesma meticulously prepares her pastry for a nine-course degustation. Contributed photo

blocks.text: It’s the same for Sze, who found herself having to look up certain words that her assistant, who is a culinary school graduate, would often use in the kitchen.
Both women had learned cooking by doing.
This time, both wanted the formal grounding to match what they already knew.
Before the resorts and the noodle houses, Ledesma and Sze were just two girls who had something to sell.
For Sze, learning to cook began with learning to taste. At home, her parents would ask what a dish needed: more salt, more sweetness, a better balance.
She was often asked to try the dish, identify what was missing, then add it herself. That early practice of testing and adjusting became a way of thinking about food.
Sze was eight when a move to Davao had her wanting to help earn money for tuition and personal expenses.

She made yema and polvoron, learning to craft these sweets through family and necessity. While this was her first foray into the culinary world, she attests that they aren’t really considered cooking.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze checks her food creation. Photo by: Jade Tan/Rappler

blocks.text: Years later, under the name Manila Flavorful Asian Favorites, Sze would run catering services and work on party trays and food carts from a studio condominium.
In peak periods, she cooked 40 to 80 trays a day, starting as early as 2 or 3 am.
It was a lot to prepare all on her own. Her husband would come home from work and face the pile of dishes at the sink, waiting to be washed.
The work filled the small space. Sze recalled cooking until late at night, with dishes and cookware covering the floor from 3 in the morning until 10 at night.
Ledesma’s first kitchen memories had her standing beside her parents and grandmother, watching them cook, tasting the food and being handed broth while the pots were still going.
In second grade, like Sze, she made sweets to sell to her classmates.

“When I was in Grade 2, I started making yema, I started making polvoron, I started making turon. I learned how to make money at a very young age because I love making food, also so I could sell them.”
Later on, while living independently with housemates who did not cook, she made a dish of ampalaya with eggs and shared it with them.
Her housemates would tell her that it tastes different, and their enjoyment encouraged her to keep experimenting with food.
“So there, when people eat my food, it makes me feel different and happy,” Ledesma shared.

blocks.caption: Joanna Ledesma cooks for her family. Contributed photo

blocks.text: Her love for cooking grew from family. Ledesma’s grandmother had a restaurant; her parents ran businesses, including a grocery and salon, and cooked at home.
In Bolinao, seafood, sea salt, and fermented fish are part of their local food landscape.

So early on, Ledesma built food businesses in the Philippines and Malaysia. She also traveled through Southeast Asia, taking short cooking courses and seeking local families who could teach her the food of their communities.
In Malaysia, she also put up a Kopi Kubo in Kuala Lumpur after staying there for two years.

In Bali, Indonesia, she went to a village in 2023 and asked her driver’s mother to show her how they made babi guling, which is similar to the Philippines’ lechon. She wanted to understand not only the recipe, but the traditions behind it.
But Ledesma graduated in finance from St. Louis University, shaped by a family that’s strongly into commerce.

In Makati, she sold healthy juices, then built Simone’s original snacks, fruits, vegetables, and meat dried into jerky. She worked the market for two to three years until she knew every vendor in the aisles and navigated the crate-stacked chaos.
Ledesma did it all, running two businesses in two countries, while raising two children.
Sze’s decision to open Nam Jai came while she was in her first trimester of pregnancy, tired of managing tray orders alone.
“The only thing that I craved during the pregnancy was having my own restaurant,” she joked.
Ledesma, meanwhile, shared it was her husband’s idea to put up a coffee shop on a lot they had bought along a highway, partly so he could have his coffee on long drives.
Amid their growing success, both Sze and Ledesma felt the need to go back to school.
At 40, with two kids and multiple businesses, Ledesma initially hesitated until she found the Center for Culinary Arts’ (CCA) professional weekend program, which had people around her age.
She traveled to Manila from Bolinao every week. During the finals, she lived in Manila for an entire month to fully focus.

blocks.caption: Chef Marco critiques the dishes prepared by students Joanna and Jeremaine at CCA. Photo by Jade Tan/Rappler

blocks.text: Sze had already taken introductory courses at CCA, but wanted more depth.
Her progression included signing up for Kitchen Discovery, Food and Culture Appreciation, Fundamentals of Culinary, and ProChef.
The credential question followed her there.
“Being a good cook is not enough,” Sze said. “People will still ask you, ‘Culinary graduate ka?’ San ka nag-aral? (Are you a culinary graduate? Where did you study?)”
The school experience tested Sze and Ledesma in various ways.
The pressure weighed in for Sze as she juggled culinary school and her business along with her pregnancy.
During classes, Sze kept her phone so she could check the CCTV and monitor the restaurant’s staff and customer flow.

blocks.caption: Jeremaine Sze opens Nam Jai Thai Noodle House.Contributed photo
Jeremaine Sze and her husband pose for a maternity photo shoot during her CCA graduation. Contributed photo

blocks.text: For Ledesma, the lesson of formal technique arrived through heat. She was not used to a kitchen with many stoves running at once, or to washing and cleaning her own station, after being accustomed to directing operations and focusing on menu development and recipe research.
“Hindi ako sanay, mainit sa kitchen (I’m not used to it, it’s hot in the kitchen),” Ledesma shared.
But completing the work gives her a sense of accomplishment: “Oh, kaya ko pala (Oh, so I can actually do it).”
At Nam Jai’s kitchen, Sze’s culinary school habits became evident, from the color-coded cutting boards to sanitation practices and house rules.
Sze feels fully stepped into her role as a chef, confident enough to direct experienced staff, lead training, and instill cooking discipline.
“Yung seven to eight hours na broth [of khao soi], I don’t do shortcuts,” she said. “So, parang in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.”
(The seven to eight hours of cooking the broth of khao soi, I don’t do shortcuts. So, like in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.)

blocks.caption: Person, Chef, Clothing
CCA graduate Joanna Ledesma learns that culinary education complements food entrepreneurship. Photos from CCA

blocks.text: Ledesma’s kitchens also had school imprints: knife skills, ingredient evaluation, seafood technique — all of them also taught to staff and family, quietly correcting provincial habits, like how shrimp shouldn’t be boiled too long or else they turn rubbery.
Her signature dishes involve the fresh seafood of her beach town; her philosophy: all healthy, organic, pesticide-free, MSG-free, non-GMO cooking.
For Ledesma, one of the satisfying moments at graduation was when she could finally call herself a chef.
“Don’t hesitate,” Ledesma said. “If you have the means of doing culinary, please do it. It will improve you a lot, physically, mentally, and emotionally.” – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

articles.title: Adiong: Firm linked to Sara Duterte's husband a 'national security concern'
articles.summary: The company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, raises concerns beyond questions about unexplained assets, including potential national security…

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 4:26pm

The company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, raises concerns beyond questions about unexplained assets, including potential national security implications, House prosecution spokesperson Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said on Sunday.
“This goes beyond non-disclosure or unexplained assets in her SALN. It goes to the very core of national security concerns,” Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.
Adiong made the statement after the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) confirmed that a company linked to Duterte and Carpio received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
According to a table the AMLC presented, P315.93 million came from mainland China, while P3.39 million came from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Duterte questioned the allegations, asking whether doing business with China was prohibited on national security grounds.

“So ano ba talaga? Bawal ba talaga ang negosyo with China kasi it is a national security risk? Parang nakakahiya na nga yung drug haul na papuntang Pilipinas galing Laos and Thailand, tapos eto pa tayo na nagsasabing, ‘Naku, it’s a national security risk na magnegosyo with China.’ Nagiging troublemaker of Southeast Asia tayo,” Duterte said.

(So what is it, then? Is doing business with China really prohibited because it poses a national security risk? It is already embarrassing that there is a drug shipment bound for the Philippines from Laos and Thailand, and now we are saying that doing business with China is a national security risk. We are becoming the troublemaker of Southeast Asia.)
Adiong said Philippine authorities should investigate possible money laundering activities involving funds from China.

“Ito ba ang rason kung bakit ang Bise Presidente ay sinasabi niyang troublemaker ang Pilipinas despite the fact na ang China ay continuous ang mga aggressive na mga activity diyan sa West Philippine Sea? Hindi man lang siya makapagsabi ng kanyang posisyon, na makapag-call out these illegal activities committed by China,” Adiong said.

(Is this the reason why the Vice President is calling the Philippines a troublemaker despite China’s continued aggressive activities in the West Philippine Sea? She cannot even state her position or call out China's illegal activities.)
“Ito ba ang rason kung bakit nasasabi niya ’yun? Kasi may mga kumpanya niya, as declared sa kanyang SALN, na tumatanggap ng remittances galing sa China,” he added.
(Is this the reason she is saying that? Because companies linked to her, as declared in her SALN, are receiving remittances from China.)

In a separate statement, House prosecution adviser Robert Ace Barbers said authorities should examine whether China was exploiting the Philippines’ political divisions amid Duterte’s impeachment proceedings to advance its interests.

“Is China simply pursuing its aggressive maritime agenda, or is it also taking advantage of our political divisions to weaken our resolve? These are questions our national security officials must examine,” Barbers said.
“The impeachment proceedings are an internal constitutional process. China has no business exploiting our political differences to advance its interests in our waters,” he added.
Earlier this month, the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) reported that 101 Chinese vessels had been monitored across several West Philippine Sea (WPS) features in September 2026.
The figure was higher than the 56 Chinese vessels monitored in the disputed area in August.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: When the Cordillera danced down Session Road
articles.summary: The Festival of Festivals turns Session Road into a showcase of the region’s diverse cultural traditions

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The gongs came first, then the colors.

Then came women balancing clay pots on their heads, men carrying shields and spears, dancers in woven skirts and feathered headgear, baskets of grain, bamboo, chants, prayer movements, and stories that usually live several mountain roads apart.
On October 17, they all met on Session Road.
The 5th Cordillera Festival of Festivals brought together the region’s six provinces and two cities, turning downtown Baguio into a living picture of the Cordillera’s diversity.

blocks.caption: BELIEF. Tabuk City performers present Gabbok, a traditional Kalinga thanksgiving associated with the birth of a first child, during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals in Baguio City on October 17, 2026. The performance used chants, music, dance, and scenes of family life to express gratitude, b…

blocks.text: More than 500 performers joined the parade and cultural showcase, moving from the Melvin Jones area through Harrison Road, Magsaysay Avenue, and Session Road before gathering near Post Office Park.

Abra brought the Kawayan Festival, while Apayao presented Say-am. Benguet was represented by Kabayan’s Bindiyan, Ifugao by Gotad ad Ifugao, Kalinga by Pasil’s Tachok-Salip, Mountain Province by Lang-ay featuring Pasuk-ey, Baguio by Panagbenga, and Tabuk City by Gabbok.
It was easy to be dazzled. The more interesting part was figuring out what everyone was actually dancing about.

blocks.caption: TRADITION. fugao performers showcase Gotad ad Ifugao during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, traditional dances, agricultural symbols, and stories of ancestry, abundance, and community to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Abra’s performance highlighted bamboo craftsmanship, resilience, and the intersection of the province’s lowland and Tingguian, or Itneg, traditions.
Apayao’s Say-am was about thanksgiving, community, gongs, song, dance, and shared celebration.
Kabayan’s Bindiyan brought the pulse of the gangsa and a circle dance tied to victory, thanksgiving, and communal life.
Ifugao’s Gotad turned part of Session Road into a scene of ritual and daily life, with chants, rice, agricultural tools, baskets, woven objects, and movements tied to ancestry and abundance.
Pasil’s Tachok-Salip featured gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and movements that spoke of joy, unity, and connection to the land.
Mountain Province presented Lang-ay through Pasuk-ey, a Central Bontoc thanksgiving tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual.
Tabuk’s Gabbok celebrated the birth of a first child.
Baguio’s Panagbenga performance drew on the story of Bangan, an Ibaloy woman whose offering to Kabunian is linked to the Benguet pine.
Put all eight together and one thing becomes obvious.
Mayor Benjamin Magalong said that even people who have lived in the region for years still have plenty to learn about one another.
“We may be neighbors, but our customs, celebrations, languages, traditions, and histories are not all the same,” he said.
Baguio itself, Magalong noted, has long been shaped by people from across the region who came to the city and eventually called it home.
“So much of the region is already present here in our city,” he said. “And today, that becomes even more visible.”

blocks.caption: DANCE. Mountain Province performers present the Lang-ay Festival featuring Pasuk-ey: The Thanksgiving Summer Fest during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, prayer dances, and a Central Bontoc tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual, to Session Road.…

blocks.text: There were, naturally, phones everywhere. Session Road gave people plenty of reasons to point them.
But the Festival of Festivals was never meant to be reduced to a reel of costumes, choreography, and pretty pictures.
Department of Tourism (DOT) – Cordillera Regional Director Jovita Ganongan said the dances, garments, and traditions on display should be understood for what they are.
“Our festivals are not merely performances of our culture,” she said. “They are expressions of our identity, living stories of our ancestors, and a legacy we must carry forward.”
Ganongan also said the region’s cultural differences should not be mistaken for division.
“We may be different in our traditions and expressions of culture, but we are united through our heritage and our pride in who we are,” she said.

It is easy to turn culture into something decorative on a festival stage. But Cordillera traditions are tied to land, kinship, farming, ritual, memory, peace, conflict, survival, and belief. Strip away those meanings and what remains may still look beautiful, but it is no longer the whole story.
Baguio Representative Mauricio Domogan said the harder part comes after the applause.
“When the music subsides and the parade has passed, our responsibility to our heritage must endure,” he said.

blocks.caption: ABRA. Abra performers showcase the Abrenian Kawayan Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing bamboo traditions and the shared heritage of the province’s lowland and Tingguian or Itneg communities to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Tourism without losing the plot
The Festival of Festivals is also a tourism event, and nobody was pretending otherwise.
DOT Secretary Judilyn Quiachon said the Cordillera has a distinct place in Philippine tourism because of its mountains, rice terraces, food, crafts, and living cultural traditions.
But she said more visitors should not be the only goal.
Tourism should create opportunities for local businesses, farmers, artisans, guides, accommodation providers, and other workers while respecting Indigenous cultures and protecting the environment.
The point, she said, is for communities to “participate meaningfully in and benefit from tourism development.”

Ganongan put it more plainly during an earlier briefing. Tourism should “entertain and educate, not exploit,” create livelihoods without sacrificing identity, and welcome visitors without pushing communities to the margins of their own stories.

How do you invite people to look without turning culture into spectacle? How do you make traditions visible without reducing them to content? How do you welcome tourism without asking communities to perform a version of themselves that outsiders find easier to consume?
But for that morning, the people carrying the traditions remained in the middle of the frame.

blocks.caption: TRADITION. Kalinga performers from Pasil showcase the Tachok-Salip Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and traditions of celebration, unity, and connection to the land to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: A Cordillera too big for one photo
Women moved in measured steps beneath foliage headdresses while young men struck gongs behind them.

Rice was winnowed in the middle of Session Road. Farming tools became props but also reminders of where many of these traditions begin. Clay pots rose above dancers’ heads. Wooden bulul figures sat among grain and baskets. Men crouched low with gongs, then sprang back into movement.
Elders danced beside students. Older women carried traditions beside younger performers learning to inherit them.
Some spectators knew exactly what they were seeing. Others were encountering these practices for the first time.
The festival did not ask Abra to look like Kalinga, Ifugao to move like Benguet, or Mountain Province to tell the same story as Apayao.
Domogan summed it up in one line: “Identity does not require uniformity.”
By noon, the gongs had quieted. Performers were resting, spectators were drifting away, and Session Road was slowly becoming Session Road again.
After five years in Baguio, the Festival of Festivals will leave the city for the first time in 2027, with Kalinga set to host. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Whole streets in Paris ‘devastated’ by protests, says mayor, as France demonstrations continue – Europe live
articles.summary:
France’s worst protests in years saw buildings set ablaze across the country and record numbers of people arrested

In case you are still catching up with the news from yesterday, my…

blocks.text: Opening summary
France is recovering after its worst protests in years saw buildings attacked and set ablaze across the country.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in the demonstrations on Saturday, which began with protests from students over the cost of living.
However violent fringe groups came out in support of the students, which saw events spiralling out of control.
Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said.
Meanwhile in Limoges, central France, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.

Authorities in France are now waiting to see if protests will go into another day. The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris, where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
We will be following events in France and bringing you any reaction as it comes in.
Key events

items: 32m agoRecord numbers arrested in Paris
42m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: In case you are still catching up with the news from yesterday, my colleagues Kim Willsher and William Christou have this report.

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.

Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt.

Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
Record numbers arrested in Paris
Police in Paris arrested a “record figure” of 855 people during the protests on Saturday.
Agence France-Presse reported the number detained was the highest ever for a single event.
The figure forms part of the 1,200 arrested across France, as prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police had been hurt in clashes.
Meanwhile Deputy Mayor of Paris Lamia El Aaraje said the capital had been hit by “a level of violence that I believe we had never seen before”.

articles.title: Freeland believes her resignation led to better outcome for Trudeau, allowing him to exit before likely defeat
articles.summary: Former finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland believes her resignation — which spurred Justin Trudeau to step down — was ultimately a good outcome for the former prime minister…

image.caption: Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland gets a shout-out from then-prime minister Justin Trudeau during a caucus meeting on Parliament Hill in Ottawa in April 2024. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Former finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland believes her resignation — which spurred Justin Trudeau to step down — was ultimately a good outcome for the former prime minister given his plummeting popularity.
In CBC interview, former finance minister defends her record and says history will look kindly on Trudeau

While her book, Unreliable Boyfriend, is meant to be a guide for dealing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, it also outlines how her political relationship with Trudeau declined in the final months of his government.

Freeland writes that the prime minister informed her in a Zoom call that he would be replacing her as finance minister just days before she was set to deliver the government's fall economic statement in late 2024.
She abruptly stepped down the same day the statement was to be tabled in Parliament. Trudeau resigned a few weeks later.

items: In Unreliable Boyfriend, Chrystia Freeland details the rift between her and Trudeau

blocks.text: Her book outlines how a conversation with former Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien a month earlier helped her make the ultimate decision to leave.
Speaking to CBC's The Sunday Magazine, Freeland detailed another conversation she had with Chrétien in the wake of the blow-up.

"Prime minister Chrétien said … in resigning, it was ultimately a better outcome for Canada, for the Liberal Party — and also ultimately for prime minister Trudeau because it allowed him not to lead our party to defeat," Freeland told host Piya Chattopadhyay.
"I think that is a very wise observation."

The Conservatives held a huge lead in the polls over Trudeau's Liberals during the final year of his tenure. Mark Carney won the Liberal leadership race to replace Trudeau and led the party to another election win in 2025.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Chrystia Freeland rises to present the federal budget in the House of Commons in Ottawa as Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, lower right, listens on April 16, 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Freeland defends record as finance minister
Freeland had been a cabinet minister in Trudeau's government since it was first elected in 2015 and served as finance minister from the summer of 2020 until her resignation.

When asked if she felt she bore any responsibility for the fading popularity of the Trudeau government — given that the Conservative surge was driven by their focus on the economy and cost of living — she touted her record as finance minister.
LISTEN | Chrystia Freeland on The Sunday Magazine:
The Sunday Magazine43:02Chrystia Freeland talks Trump, Canada-U.S. trade war and political tenure with Trudeau
"I am very glad that as finance minister, I got us through COVID and I preserved our AAA credit rating while doing that," she said.
"We were able to return to a sustainable fiscal path. Now, that was politically hard to do, but it was absolutely the right thing to do."

Despite their political fallout, Freeland spoke kindly of her early political relationship with Trudeau. And, as she notes in her book, she argued that history will look kindly on Trudeau — but added that she wished he had stepped down earlier.
Justin Trudeau and Chrystia Freeland over the years

She insisted multiple times in the interview that Unreliable Boyfriend is "not a book about Justin Trudeau." But she didn't directly answer if she had reached out to her former boss during the writing process.

"I chose what I wrote really carefully. It was important for me to be authentic and to be open. But this really is a book about me and a book about my ideas and my view of where we should go," she said.
"It's not a salacious story."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
Interview produced by Sarah-Joyce Battersby

articles.title: Doing the dishes and riding the subway? Why the royals keep trying to look relatable
articles.summary: Members of the Royal Family are offering glimpses into their everyday lives, the most recent examples of attempts to deal with a fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to…

image.caption: Catherine, Princess of Wales, left, laughs as she talks with Lynda Jones, right, who offered her a potato chip at a weekly lunch club in Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. During that visit, Catherine mentioned to seniors that she and Prince William do the dishes together at home. (Arthur Ed

blocks.text: It all seemed a bit prosaic, really, chatting about doing the dishes with her husband or riding on the subway with her daughter.

But there was Catherine, Princess of Wales, telling seniors how she and Prince William share the washing-up duties, and a few days later, taking a trip on the London Underground with Princess Charlotte.

Beyond that glimpse into their everyday lives, though, these recent moments reflect an attempt to deal with a longstanding and more fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to appear relatable to a public that lives far beyond royal walls.
"The monarchy isn't trying to convince us that William and Catherine are ordinary people," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.
"It's about trying to convince us that despite extraordinary circumstances, they experience the same human concerns as everybody else."
Efforts to do that convincing have long been a priority for monarchies throughout Europe.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, sits with residents onboard a West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group, during a visit to Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. (Arthur Edwards/AFP/Getty Images)

"Since … the political upheavals of the 19th century, which saw various monarchs … losing their thrones … there was a real consciousness that you no longer needed just the support of the elite, you needed to be relatable," said Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, in an interview.
"Queen Victoria writes her highland journal — suitably sanitized — but that's an attempt to make herself relatable."

What's thought of as relatable nearly 200 years ago differs from what William and Catherine and other working royals may try to do or show today. But the overall significance is the same, Rowbotham suggests.
"Relatability is something that modern monarchies, certainly modern European monarchies, see as genuinely important," she said.

"Particularly at a time when people are worried about money, when people are questioning government actions over taxes … the fact that yes, they live in a lavish house, but they live ordinary lives in a lavish house … that's the impression they want to give, that they don't have live-in staff, they're not surrounded by flunkies and footmen."
As much as there is that desire to appear relatable, there is little to suggest it can ultimately eliminate the actual separation between the monarchy and the public.

This 1969 photo is one of a series taken to show the informal life of Prince Charles, centre, as he sits with Queen Elizabeth, background centre, Prince Philip, second from left, Prince Edward, left, Princess Anne, background, and then Prince Andrew, right, at Sandringham House, in Sandringham, England. (The Associated Press)
"There will always be distance between the monarchy and the people," said Vovk.
"But all of [it], stretching from Queen Victoria up to William and Catherine is about trying to close as much of the distance as they can that is within their control."
And there's a basic reason behind that, Vovk suggests.
"The monarchy's relevance, its viability, is now predicated on its perceived relatability and accessibility," he said.

"People don't want a Royal Family that is distant and isolated and feels unfamiliar. They want a Royal Family that they feel they can connect with, that they feel like if they were to bump into them on the street, they could just go up to them and talk to them."
That, however, creates something of a paradox.

"If you strip away all of the pomp and the pageantry and some of the mystique around royalty, it raises the question of what makes it so special, anyway? Why have it at all?" Vovk said. "So it is a balancing act."

Pomp and pageantry are on full display as King Charles, left, and Queen Camilla, right, make their way along the Mall following their coronation on May 6, 2023, in London, England. (Charles McQuillan/The Associated Press)
Other factors can play into the monarchy's focus on relatability at any given time.

Queen Victoria's seclusion, particularly after the death of her husband, Prince Albert, drove concerns about relatability during her reign. Rowbotham sees another circumstance closely connected to the monarch at play right now.
"We don't know how long Charles is going to be around, given that he's in his 70s, given that he is still being treated for cancer," she said.
"This time, it's a question of assuring the monarchy's survival by making it clear that there is an heir who is well-prepared and ready to take over the duty.
"That's why I think … they're paying so much attention to the whole issue" of relatability, Rowbotham said.

items: With move to 'forever home,' Prince and Princess of Wales could offer hint of 'more egalitarian' monarchy

blocks.text: Vovk sees a greater level of transparency from the current royals compared to previous generations when it comes to relatability.

"We're seeing the curtain being pulled back on the aspects of royal life that are no different or at least have minimal difference from the average person — so, you know, siblings bickering, not liking doing chores, spouses sharing domestic responsibilities."
On the constitutional or political side of the monarchy, however, he sees less revelation.

"There's still some degree of gatekeeping going on here with what amount of royal life is being disclosed and what isn't. That will always be the case with something that is connected with the political life of the nation."
Passing a robot controller to a prince

Benjamin Santiago, left, teaches Prince Edward, right, how to drive a robot using a controller at Queen's Park in Toronto on Oct. 2. (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)
Benjamin Santiago had never had an experience like it.

"It's not every day that you get to give a robot controller to royalty and teach them how to drive it," the Grade 12 student at St. Joseph's Catholic High School in London, Ont., said in an interview.
Benjamin, a 17-year-old member of the school robotics team, had that opportunity earlier this month when he passed the controller to Prince Edward, the Duke of Edinburgh, at an event in Toronto.

The gathering that drew education leaders, school board representatives, industry partners and students to Queen's Park highlighted the recent announcement by the provincial Ministry of Education to expand access to the Duke of Edinburgh Award program to schools across Ontario. That comes as the award, founded by Edward's late father, Prince Philip, is evolving and working to blend trades and skills-based experiences into public education to boost opportunities for young Canadians.

"It was amazing. I'm super grateful," Benjamin said of his opportunity to meet Edward. "The prince was super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students."
In the royal encounter, Benjamin saw the potential to boost support for an area of education close to his heart.

Benjamin says Prince Edward was 'super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students.' (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)

"If someone like the prince can feel the controller and feel how it is to be an engineer in high school and then later on become an engineer in post-secondary … the funding towards programs like robotics may increase."
Edward has had a longstanding interest in youth and promoting opportunities for them, something that has been a frequent focus on his visits to Canada.

"He really took the time to really focus his attention on the students, which is something that I really personally admired about this, but also to make sure that every student felt seen and heard," Laura Briscoe, senior director for business development, communications and experiential education for the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada, said in an interview.

"He wants to know the realities of youth in Canada and how the award can support their lifelong learning and development, and I found him to be very responsive and open to hearing feedback, whether it's constructive feedback, what are the barriers, where are the gaps, what are we missing?"

items: More 'soft power signals': On heels of King's visit, Prince Edward takes week-long trip to P.E.I., Ontario
Prince Edward makes royal visit to Canada — pandemic-style

blocks.text: The Queen's Park gathering was a "wonderful experience" for everyone there, said Kathy Cepo, Benjamin's chemistry teacher and one of his robotics coaches.
"The prince was so engaged with these students and they felt like they were the only people in the room," she said in an interview.
"He was praising them the entire time and so proud of them."
They meet again
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace in London on Wednesday. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)
Few world leaders have shaken hands with King Charles as often as the president of Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy was back in the U.K. this week, meeting Charles at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience," Zelenskyy posted afterward on X.
"It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance provided by the United Kingdom."

It was his third meeting with the King this year, and came as the U.K. doubled down on support for Ukraine and called for its international partners to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to respect the U.S. call for an energy ceasefire.
The King meeting with Zelenskyy "on a bit of a consistent basis is a way of … reaffirming Britain's overall support for Ukraine, even though governments are changing," said Vovk.
"It's a way to reassure President Zelenskyy that the United Kingdom stands with Ukraine."
While a monarch is meant to be above politics, meeting with Zelenskyy would also come at the request of the U.K. government.
"The King isn't being party political, taking sides. He's doing his constitutional duty," said Rowbotham.
Prince Harry and Meghan step out in Nottingham

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, and Prince Harry, right, greet well-wishers as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity that offers a wide range of creative activities, sports, mentoring and youth development programs, in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)
They aren't official working members of the Royal Family anymore.

But the casual passerby could be forgiven for being a bit confused Thursday as Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, carried out events connected with their private charitable interests in the city where they did their first public outing as an engaged couple nearly a decade ago. It was their first joint appearance in public since they returned to the U.K. from California in late August.
"It's great to be back," Harry said. "Wonderful and great to be back ⁠in Nottingham, too."

items: Charles confirms Harry and Meghan to remain non-working royals after their return to U.K.

blocks.text: They began by visiting a recording studio run by a youth and community charity that has received support from a 1.1-​million-pound ($2.1-million Cdn) donation announced by Harry last year.

At their next stop at the Himmah charity, which tackles food poverty, Meghan was reunited with ​four contributors to a charity cookbook released to raise funds in the wake of London's 2017 Grenfell Tower fire disaster. She had donated 10,000 pounds ($18,800 Cdn) from the book's proceeds to help the Himmah hub.
Thursday's visit was the first pre-arranged and advertised occasion since their return, Rowbotham said, but it was not an official royal event.
Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K.

"However, it was carefully arranged to ensure media reportage and a suitable turnout of sympathetic public by choosing a location — Nottingham — which was … where they were for their first post engagement royal visit."
But it was on a much different scale, she said.
"No local dignitaries were there in official capacity."
Vovk saw the visit as their first outing as part of "the new Sussex court."

He also sees the potential of a "problem of optics" for the monarchy where "Harry and Meghan are engaging in activities that to the average observer look really more or less the same [as] what the monarchy does."
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, visit the Himmah Hub in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/The Associated Press)
Vovk expects to see an escalation in public appearances and informal events from the senior working royals.

"I think the monarchy is now going to have to pick up the pace in terms of the kinds of engagements and public accessibility they're doing just in order to keep that clear distinction between Harry and Meghan [having] titles but they are technically private individuals from a legal, constitutional perspective," he said.

items: Why Prince Harry and Meghan face more challenges after their return to the U.K.
The 'shockwaves' of Prince Harry and Meghan's return to the U.K.

blocks.text: The biggest danger and concern for the royals, he said, is "that the brand itself could be misappropriated, misrepresented, in a way that has never really been a factor before."
Rowbotham doesn't see a threat to the institution itself, although she expects it will be discussed as such.
Royally quotable
"We like sitting quietly and reading. Occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, I'll hear him roaring with laughter about something."
— Queen Camilla, in a television documentary, offering some insight into the reading habits of her and her husband, King Charles.
Royal reads

Catherine, Princess of Wales, third from left, and Prince William, third from right, help behind the till during a visit to an Ikea store in Belfast, Northern Ireland, on Oct. 9. (Phil Noble/Getty Images)

British police say search ‌warrants they secured to search properties linked to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been issued unlawfully and must be quashed, but said the investigation into King Charles's younger brother was ongoing. [CBC]

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced a 1.8-million-pound ($3.4-million Cdn) bill to cover repair and restoration of his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor after the lease was officially surrendered. King Charles reportedly covered some of the costs. [The Guardian]
King Charles spoke of his "special connection" to Wales while delivering an address to the Welsh Parliament. [The Independent]

Zara Tindall has opened up about the tough-love upbringing she received from Princess Anne and Mark Phillips — including being told she would get no help when she decided to follow her parents into top-level equestrian sport. [Daily Mail]
The Prince and Princess of Wales met hundreds of royal fans in south Belfast as part of a surprise visit to Northern Ireland. [Belfast Telegraph]
Prince William brought traffic to a halt just down the road from Buckingham Palace to play cricket with some of the game's biggest names. [The Independent]
Prince William joins cricket stars for an informal game on The Mall in London, England, on Tuesday, in the leadup to the annual Earthshot Prize awards in Mumbai next month. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

articles.title: They don't make instant coffee like they used to. It's getting gourmet now
articles.summary: In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up,…

image.caption: Just Us! in Halifax has been selling premium instant coffee for over 15 years. But over the past couple years, it's seen a big boost in sales. (Harrison Newman Jardine)

blocks.text: Cost of Living

In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up, thanks to better quality, some social media trends, and advancements in instant coffee technology.
Instant coffee sales have increased across Canada in recent years
LISTEN | Why more people are drinking instant coffee:
Cost of Living5:23Instant coffee is having a moment

In a world of fancy espresso machines, gourmet blends and cold brews, instant coffee has often been considered to be at the bottom of the proverbial coffee barrel. But the powder is getting a glow-up, thanks to better quality, social media trends and advancements in instant coffee technology.
"It's having a moment," said Joey Pittoello, general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. "I think people have discovered that instant coffee can be of much better quality now."
More brewers are choosing to highlight instant coffee, from big brands such as Starbucks, to smaller roasters like Just Us!, in part because they are seeing an increased demand for it.

At Just Us!, which has been selling instant coffee for over 15 years, instant coffee sales have grown around 15 per cent in the last two years, says Pittoello, with other coffee companies such as Eight Ounce Coffee and Canadian Heritage Coffee Roasters in Calgary reporting similar increases in recent years.
According to a 2025 Agricultural Canada report, instant coffee sales totalled $330 million in Canada in 2024, up 10 per cent from the previous year.
"Instant coffee is undergoing the same transformation as a lot of coffee drinks," said Robert Carter, a food industry analyst and the president of the Coffee Association of Canada.
"There's more premiumization that's taking place. And I think that's resulting in an increase in consumption."

Social media trends are also improving instant coffee's rep. There's the Dalgona coffee trend, popularized during the pandemic, which is a whipped drink made by whisking instant coffee, sugar and hot water, then putting it over milk.
People are also using instant coffee to make lattes or iced coffees at home. Additionally, Pittoello says people use it in baking, or in seasoning when barbecuing.
"It's easy to make interesting sweet milky drinks with instant coffee. You just have to add it, right?" said Pittoello.
A change in quality and technology
Instant coffee isn't anything new though. Big brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House have been selling instant coffee for decades.
"I don't think it ever really went anywhere," said Pittoello.
What has changed, though, is the quality of instant coffee. Pittoello says the robusta bean, which has a simple flavour profile compared to arabica, had commonly been used to make instant coffee.
"You're enhancing the level of low quality by turning it into instant coffee and that's really what defined instant coffee for decades," said Pittoello.
Joey Pittoello is the general manager of the coffee roaster Just Us! in Halifax. (Harrison Newman Jardine)
Now more specialty roasters are using better beans to make their instant coffee. Just Us! uses arabica, as does Starbucks.

But that's not the only reason you're seeing specialty coffee shops selling their own instant coffee. Josh Hockin, head of coffee at Eight Ounce Coffee in Calgary, says it's easier than ever to manufacture it, thanks to advancements in technology.

Mainstream brands like Nescafé and Maxwell House make large amounts of instant coffee through a process called spray drying, which involves brewing coffee as strong as possible, then spraying that coffee into a heated chamber, creating the instant coffee powder.

But Hockin says a better quality coffee can be made by brewing the coffee then freeze-drying it instead. Years ago, the machine to do so would cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and was as big as a shipping container.
Now, he says the machines cost about $3,000 to $4,000 Cdn, and can plug into the wall.
"It's not cheap to do, but it's certainly way less expensive than it would have been in the past," said Hockin.
Instant coffee jars sit on display in a Tesco supermarket on July 6, 2022 in Northwich, England. More specialty roasters are now offering their own take on instant coffee. (Getty Images)
Paying a premium

According to Robert Carter, it's not that people are replacing their at-home set up with instant coffee. Rather, Carter says, instant coffee is giving people another option to enjoy one of the most consumed drinks in Canada.
"We're not seeing a cannibalization taking place. We're seeing an expansion of the types of coffee products being consumed that are different than just your traditional brewed coffee.”
Starbucks VIA Ready Brew instant coffee is offered for sale at Starbucks coffee shop back in 2009. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

And people are willing to pay a premium for that, says Hockin. He says it's the equivalent of buying a cup at a coffee shop, with some packets of four selling for $11, while some varieties sell for $42 for a six-pack.
But, he says, the quality is just as good, and it's as convenient as it gets.
"It's not their everyday cup of coffee, obviously. But they are very willing, very very willing to pay that money.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a writer and editor for CBC Radio based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.
Produced by Danielle Nerman

articles.title: Could this 93-year-old sprinter's muscles hold clues to healthy aging? Scientists think so
articles.summary: At 93, Italian sprinter Emma Mazzenga is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.

image.caption: Emma Mazzenga, 93, poses for a photo in front of some of the dozens of medals she has won for running at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)

blocks.text: At 93, Emma Maria Mazzenga still gets the jitters before a race.
"On race day, I'm very tense," she said. "People ask to interview me, and I tell them: Don't come near me until I've run."

Over the last four decades, Mazzenga has won 11 world titles, 31 European championships and 115 Italian races. She currently holds the 200-metre world record in the women's over-90 category: 50.33 seconds, set in 2024, when she was 91.
Now she is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.

Mazzenga ran as a university student in Padua, in northern Italy. She then stopped for three decades while she taught high school biology and raised two children, largely on her own after her husband died.
In 1986, when she was 53, the president of her old university running club rounded up former athletes for the growing field of masters competitions, for those over age 35.
"One by one, my friends quit," she said. "I kept going."

In this 2024 file photo, a then-90-year-old Mazzenga shows her membership card for the Italian Athletics Federation, ahead of a race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy. It shows her birthdate: Aug. 1, 1933. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)
She still trains three times a week, mostly short repeats of 50 to 200 metres. Slow jogging bores her.
What drives her isn't winning, Mazzenga said. In Italy, she has no rivals in her age category. "I come first because I have to. I'm the only one," she said. "I can't get any emotion out of that."
So she races the clock instead. "If I win with a mediocre time, it gives me no satisfaction."
Her proudest moment is still her first world title, the 400-metre W75 race at the World Masters Athletics Championships in Sacramento, Calif., won in 2011.
"There were just a handful of us Italians. I found myself alone on the podium," Mazzenga recalled.
Watch Emma Mazzenga, 93, compete in 100-metre race
From VO2 to muscle fibres
But eventually, her performances drew a different audience: Scientists.
Two years ago, Antonio La Torre, a scientist at the University of Milan and technical director of Italy’s athletic federation, tipped off two researchers who were studying how the body ages.

"We were told there was this woman who was able to run 200 metres in a very short time," said Martino Franchi, an associate professor of human physiology at the University of Padua. "But it was her age that we were really interested in."

items: 'Superagers' reveal how to stay sharp as you get older

blocks.text: Mazzegna became the most extreme case in a broader, two-year project called Trajector-Age, which tracked how muscles, nerves, heart and metabolism change in people over 50 to see whether exercise can slow decline.
Researchers from several Italian universities and the University of Wisconsin-Madison put Mazzenga through a gruelling cycling test and took biopsies from her thigh.
Mazzenga, then 90, competes in the 100-metre W90 category race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy, on May 4, 2024. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

Franchi says Mazzenga's maximal oxygen consumption is comparable to that of someone in their 50s. Also known as a VO2 max, it represents the greatest amount of oxygen a body can take in and use — a key measure of cardiovascular fitness.
"And she's 90," he said. "This is fantastic."

The bigger surprise was inside her muscles, said Franchi. Mazzenga has lost some of the fast-twitch fibres used for explosive movement, although fewer than expected. But her slow-twitch fibres — the ones that resist fatigue — are extraordinary.
"They are as big as a girl in her 20s," he said. "That's unique."
Martino Franchi gestures toward a screen showing a microscopic view of muscle fibres at his lab at the University of Padua, in Italy. (CBC)
Researchers think those unusually large fibres may help her hold her pace and compensate, at least partly, for the fast fibres lost with age.
Aging has happened, Franchi said, "but in a slower way." And so many years of training means that her body runs almost on auto-pilot when her feet hit the track.

The research was published earlier this year as two cases in the Journal of Applied Physiology, with a rendition of a Mazzenga landing on the cover. Lead scientist Marta Colosio received an award for the work at the American Physiology summit.
The team is now analyzing a second round of biopsies, along with genetic and molecular data, trying to tease apart what Mazzenga inherited versus what decades of training may have preserved.
Mazzenga walks with Martino Franchi, one of the researchers who has studied the 93-year-old's muscles and athletic performance to glean new insights into human aging. (CBC)

items: She just won 3 powerlifting medals. Oh, and she's 82 | The Moment

blocks.text: 'A bit of a rarity'
Mazzenga has her own theory. "I always say that if I had been sitting on the sofa, I would have aged differently."
With the running came fame — eventually. "No one paid much attention to me in my 80s, but after 90, yes," she jokes. "They look at me as a bit of a rarity."
She now speaks regularly at public events, most recently at la Repubblica's Festival di Salute, an annual health festival that draws Nobel laureates, scientists and sports champions.
As friends die and family members get busy with their own lives, Mazzenga says those connections — along with her masters teammates — matter almost as much as the training.
Mazzenga shows off her first pair of track shoes, when she first took to racing in her early 50s, at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)
Franchi has his own reason for pushing exercise.
During the COVID-19 lockdowns, he noticed his father, then in his 70s, struggling to get up from the sofa. So Franchi printed out graphs linking inactivity to mortality.
"I said, 'Dad, I study sarcopenia. This is it,'" said Franchi, referring to the loss of muscle mass, strength and function with age. "He got scared, so he went back to the gym."
Today, Franchi's father can pull off full lunges and hikes several times a week.

items: Clara Hughes was used to pushing her body. When menopause hit, her body pushed back
Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours

blocks.text: Franchi likes to tell the story to his students, telling them that physical activity is important — but be sure to keep doing it when you're older.
Asked what she'd tell someone 80, or even 90, thinking about taking up a sport, Mazzenga laughs. "You'd want to start a little earlier."
For those still able, she says, see a doctor, find a coach and match your body to the effort.
She herself has no plans to slow down. At a recent club final, she ran faster than she had two years earlier. "I was very pleased."
Mazzenga, centre, is seen in a photo with two fellow racers when she won the European Championship in 1998. (Megan Williams/CBC)

articles.title: ‘Nowadays, you need a lot fewer people’: Laid-off Stelco workers not alone as steel jobs disappear
articles.summary: While U.S.-owned Stelco insists its plan to lay off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., is only a temporary consequence of the Canada-U.S. trade war, new technologies and demand…

image.caption: Mike Watt, whose career at Stelco spans 20 years, stands outside Stelco Hamilton Works after receiving a layoff notice on Oct. 9. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

While U.S.-owned Stelco insists its plan to lay off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., is only a temporary consequence of the Canada-U.S. trade war, new technologies and demand dynamics are working in concert with tariff-related headwinds to compress the industry’s once-robust workforce.
Number of jobs in Canada's primary steel manufacturing industry have roughly halved since 2003
Stelco Holdings laid off 85 employees at the end of last week, according to union leader Ron Wells. The week before, he says the company issued 90 layoff notices.

While the U.S.-owned steelmaker insists its plan to lay off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., is only a temporary consequence of the Canada-U.S. trade war, new technologies and demand dynamics are working in concert with tariff-related headwinds to compress the industry’s once-robust workforce.
According to Statistics Canada, direct employment in Canada's primary steel manufacturing industry has slipped from nearly 29,000 workers in 2003 to about 14,000 workers as of July.
Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, and a 47-year veteran of Stelco, says the workforce at Stelco alone was about 14,000 strong when he started working for the company.
"To make a ton of steel nowadays, you need a lot fewer people," Wells told CBC News. "Now, it’s a lot more streamlined."

items: 'In a perfect world,' federal government would nationalize Stelco, says Hamilton union leader

blocks.text: According to U.S. regulatory filings, the total workforce of Cleveland-Cliffs — the Ohio-based owner of Stelco and North America’s largest producer of flat-rolled steel — shrank from about 30,000 employees to roughly 25,000 between Dec. 31, 2024, and Dec. 31, 2025.
This year of job cuts included about 600 layoffs in Dearborn, Mich., as Cleveland-Cliffs idled a massive blast furnace. CEO Lourenco Goncalves blamed soft demand from North American automakers.
The move prompted another 600 cuts in Minnesota to align the company’s raw ore output with reduced blast furnace demand.
An aerial image of Stelco's facility in Nanticoke, Ont. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

In late September, three months after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order applying up to 50 per cent tariffs on certain steel and aluminum imports from Canada, Stelco announced up to 500 layoffs at its two Ontario operations.
That provoked the current clash between the company and the federal government over Stelco’s obligations under the Investment Canada Act to maintain a certain number of workers in Canada.

items: Laid-off Stelco steelworkers stressed about company's future — and their own: 'We're being sold out'

blocks.text: But Stelco’s workforce isn’t the only cohort of Ontario steel workers facing job uncertainty.

Last December, Algoma Steel issued layoff notices to about 1,000 workers, nearly a third of its workforce. While the Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.-based company blamed U.S. tariffs for crushing its export competitiveness, the announcement coincided with plans to fast-track its transition to greener and less labour-intensive electric-arc furnace production.

That came after ArcelorMittal Long Products Canada announced the permanent shutdown of its Parkdale wire-drawing facility in Hamilton in June 2025. The company is a subsidiary of ArcelorMittal S.A., the world’s second-largest steel and mining company.

"Despite our best efforts, the ongoing economic challenges, increased steel imports in Canada and market conditions made it clear that we needed to reduce our operating footprint," company spokesperson Jean-Philippe Grou told CBC News at the time.
Calls to address cheaper foreign steel imports

In a letter to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly obtained by The Canadian Press, Stelco president Paul Simon complained that imports of cold-rolled and coated steel accounted for 45 per cent of market share for those products.

Wells says Ottawa is not doing enough to shield Canadian producers from cheaper foreign imports. He wants tariff-rate quotas increased to impede the flow of foreign steel competing with Canadian supply.
"There’s too much capacity coming from offshore," he said. "It dilutes the price in Canada."
'Everything is on the table' in Stelco negotiations, says industry minister

A new forecast from research firm Wood Mackenzie shows the contrast between the steel industry in the U.S. versus Canada. It predicts U.S. steel production will rise about 4.5 per cent this year, even as demand in America shrinks. Senior research analyst Tiago Vespoli sees a different reality in store for Canada.

"The increase in U.S. steel tariffs to 50 per cent has significantly disrupted … established trade flows, creating a situation in which U.S. steelmakers can increase production and market share, while Canadian producers face growing pressure on export volumes and capacity utilisation," he wrote on Thursday.
Wells says he’s encouraged by a recent uptick in spot prices for galvanized steel — a product Stelco is pivoting away from in Hamilton.

"Galvanized steel is now at $1,800 a ton in Canada, which is a vast improvement from six months ago. That’s why we find these layoffs and the idling of the cold mill and coated [steel] quite puzzling. It seemed like [prices for] coated products were starting to rebound. That’s why we believe this layoff is partially to get Carney to act and get a trade agreement," he said.
"We think it’s to get Trump to look good in the midterms, that his tariffs are working, Canadian steel workers are getting laid off."
Goncalves has openly supported Trump’s tariff agenda, a fact that has prompted blunt criticism from Joly and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
With a courtroom clash between Cliffs and Ottawa looking increasingly likely, Wells says he continues to hold onto hope that Stelco will recall the workers being laid off.
"It's hard to take them at their word anymore, to be honest with you," he said.
"I strongly believe these layoffs are temporary. I think this trade situation will get sorted out soon and our members will get back to work."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Montreal borough tightens rules on e-scooters as youth injuries skyrocket
articles.summary: The Montreal borough of Saint-Laurent has adopted a new bylaw banning electric scooters and other motorized personal mobility devices in public areas that fall within its jurisdiction. They're still…

image.caption: A person rides on an electric scooter in Toronto, on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

The Montreal borough of Saint-Laurent has adopted a new bylaw banning electric scooters and other motorized personal mobility devices in public areas that fall within its jurisdiction. They're still allowed on bike paths and streets where the maximum speed limit is less than 50 km/h.
80 scooter-related injuries in 2025 — 122 so far this year, Montreal Children's trauma director says
The Montreal borough of Saint-Laurent has adopted a new bylaw banning electric scooters and other motorized personal mobility devices in public areas that fall within its jurisdiction.
That includes city parks, trails and sidewalks.
Vana Nazarian, a city councillor for the borough, says the bylaw was adopted after a series of incidents and near misses over the summer, as the popularity of the devices continues to grow.
"We're not banning them, but we want to make sure that with the speeds that these scooters have, they stay more on places where vulnerable populations won't be at risk," she told CBC's Let's Go.
Nazarian added the borough is home to many young families and seniors, and they should be able to use parks and trails without being afraid or at risk of a collision.
She's hopeful the bylaw will force those who ride e-scooters or e-unicycles and other motorized transportation devices to use them more responsibly.

items: Boy healing from brain injury after e-scooter crash warns others of possible dangers

blocks.text: The move comes just a little over two months after Quebec decided to extend its e-scooter pilot project, even as doctors warned the rules leave children at risk.

The original pilot, introduced in 2023, allowed for anyone 14 and older to use the devices on roads where the maximum speed limit is less than 50 km/h, as well as on bike paths. Helmets are required at all times.
Those rules will still apply along with new restrictions that came into effect on July 18, including a 25 km/h speed limit for e-scooters. Exceeding that limit can result in a $200 fine by police.
14 times more injuries than in 2023
Deborah Friedman, the trauma director at the Montreal Children's Hospital, says that since the pilot came into effect, the number of e-scooter injuries have skyrocketed.
"We have seen 14 times the number of traumatic injuries related to e-scooters than we did in 2023 when it was first implemented," Friedman said.

items: Quebec is extending its e-scooter pilot project. Doctors warn the rules leave children at risk

blocks.text: In 2025, there were about 80 cases in total. So far this year, that number is 112.

Friedman, who is also the director of the Canadian Hospitals Injury Reporting and Prevention Program (CHIRPP), said the severity of injuries is also increasing, with close to 20 per cent of the cases requiring hospitalization.
"We're not talking about little cuts and bruises," she said.
The injuries include traumatic brain injuries, multiple fractures to the face, lots of facial dental trauma, complicated fractures of limbs and abdominal trauma.
Of particular concern is the age of the victims. Friedman says close to 60 per cent of the children that present at the trauma centre are under 14 years old.
"That's a problem," she said.
E-scooters spotted on Quebec highway reignite calls for stricter regulations
Stronger regulations, better enforcement needed
Friedman commended the borough of Saint-Laurent for its new bylaw and encourages other municipalities to follow suit, but she says more needs to be done at the provincial and federal levels.
Doctors across Canada have been advocating for stronger regulations and better enforcement of the rules.

Friedman said that in Quebec, they'd like to see the minimum age to use an e-scooter increased to 16, as well as a Class 6D licence made mandatory — the same licence needed to operate a vehicle like a moped.
Friedman says younger children don't have the judgment, skill level, height or control to navigate e-scooters on the road, all while following the rules.
The type of helmets used could also make a difference.
"You need to have something that's going to protect the face as well," Friedman said, saying many injuries they see are a result of children "faceplanting and ending up with profound trauma."

items: 'Exponential rise': Canadian pediatricians document severe e-scooter injuries, deaths in children, teens

blocks.text: Friedman says e-scooter manufacturers also bear some responsibility with the labelling of their products and how they are sometimes marketed as though they are toys.
With the holidays around the corner, this type of issue is of particular concern, Friedman says.
"So we're trying to work at different levels to try to sensitize the public and encourage policymakers to hear our concerns and to base decisions on real data," she said.
"Each number that I mentioned is attached to a child, which is attached to a family, which is attached to a community."

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Sunday that it has been preparing for the expected entry of Super Typhoon Champi into the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) this week.
In a news release, the agency said that as of 6 a.m., there are 4,571,390 family food packs prepositioned in its relief warehouses nationwide.
Meanwhile, 344,942 non-food items and 204,745 ready-to-eat food packs are also in stock.

"Sa pamamagitan po ng ating strategic hubs at warehouses, pinapanatili nating active ang supply chain para agad-agad nating maipahatid ang kinakailangang augmentation support kung sakali man na manghingi ng assistance ang mga komunidad na maaaring maapektuhan," DSWD Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said.

(Through our strategic hubs and warehouses, we are keeping the supply chain active so that we can immediately deliver necessary augmentation support should communities likely to be affected request assistance.)

Dumlao added that major production hubs are producing family food packs non-stop and that the agency's intensified disaster preparations align with the President's directive to maintain sufficient national stockpiles and ensure the fast delivery of relief assistance.

DSWD said it is continuing to monitor weather updates from the state weather bureau PAGASA, as the super typhoon could affect Northern Luzon, Cagayan Valley, and the northern portion of Ilocos Region toward the end of the week.

The DSWD said it is closely monitoring PAGASA weather updates on Champi, which is expected to impact Northern Luzon, Cagayan Valley, and the northern part of the Ilocos Region toward the end of the week.
