The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) have signed a data-sharing agreement to simplify the process of obtaining civil registry documents for personnel seeking benefits and other services.
The agreement allows the PCG to digitally verify PSA civil registry records for recruitment, pension claims, retirement benefits and other personnel-related transactions.

“Under the agreement, the PCG will be able to verify civil registry records maintained by the PSA for recruitment, retirement benefits, pension claims, and other personnel-related transactions,” the PCG said in a statement.

“The agreement also enables the digital processing of requests for civil registry documents, eliminating the need for PCG personnel and other concerned individuals to visit PSA service outlets in person,” it added.
The partnership aims to expedite processing and make essential government services more accessible to PCG personnel, retirees, pensioners and their dependents.

“It asks a simple question: when two institutions can work together to ease a person's burden, why should that burden remain on the person? Coordination is our responsibility. Service is our obligation. Dignity must be what every Filipino experiences when they come to government for help,” said PCG Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
articles.summary: Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

image.caption: Babis has been described as 'Trumpist' in his outlookImage: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.
The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.
What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.
The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.
Babis called the result "catastrophic."
"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.
That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.
Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform
His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.
Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

articles.title: An extraordinary life: descendant welcomes biography of woman ‘gifted’ to Queen Victoria
articles.summary:
A girl called Àìná was captured by an African king and later taken to England to become Sarah Forbes Bonetta, protege of the imperial monarch

When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s…

blocks.text: When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle’s great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.
Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter.
But while Victoria took a genuine interest in Bonetta’s welfare, making the orphan a royal protege and meeting with her over the years, their relationship was part of a bigger agenda.
Now, as a biography is published – Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta: A Yorùbá Woman in Queen Victoria’s Court – Randle has spoken of his family history.

“I don’t think a human being, who has agency, could be ‘gifted’ from one to another, but had she not been gifted to Queen Victoria, would I be here today?” said Randle, a British-Nigerian barrister from London.

blocks.caption: Bayo Randle, Bonetta’s great-great-grandson, is a barrister in London. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: The new book, by a Canadian academic, Prof Henry Lovejoy, charts how Bonetta was brought to England by Frederick Forbes, of the Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron, which was set up to enforce the abolition of the transatlantic trade.
Born in 1843 in Òkè-Òdàn, south-west Nigeria, Bonetta was originally called Àìná. Her family was killed in 1848 when her town was attacked by King Ghezo of Dahomey’s forces.
Bonetta, then five, is believed to have been captured by the agodjié – the all-female regiment depicted in the Hollywood movie The Woman King – and held at King Ghezo’s court.

blocks.caption: The book by Henry B Lovejoy. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In 1850, Forbes went to Dahomey – which is now Benin – to petition Ghezo to sign an anti-slavery treaty. The mission failed but Forbes asked Ghezo if he could take Bonetta to England.
Bonetta would go on to live a life of renown, becoming one of the most artistically represented and widely reported African women of her time. But she was never truly free.
Lovejoy’s book describes how, before Forbes arrived in England with her – giving her his own name and that of his ship, the Bonetta – he petitioned for her to be “the property of the crown”.

This meant Bonetta was “effectively indentured to Queen Victoria until age 19” under the post-abolition legal structures, Lovejoy said. Bonetta was then married off to James Pinson Labulo Davies, a merchant and philanthropist, of whom she would write: “I don’t feel a particle of love for him.”

Lovejoy’s research for the website liberatedafricans.org, developed with Kartikay Chadha, documents how, after abolition, more than 700,000 Africans “liberated” from enslavers were forced into indentures of up to 14 years “to pay for the cost of their own freedom” by governments including Britain’s.

Lovejoy claims Bonetta was at the elite end of this bonded labour system, “educated to be a missionary who would Christianise Africa”. In her lifetime her image was exploited as imperial iconography, promoting the idea that British colonialism of Africa was a “civilising mission”.

blocks.caption: Bonetta was a famous figure in 19th-century England. Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: Lovejoy, of the University of Colorado Boulder, said: “Sarah’s imagery was used to project the idea of the queen’s benevolence – at a time when ‘liberated’ Africans are being forced into indentures.”

Nonetheless, when Bonetta attended the 1858 wedding of Queen Victoria’s daughter, the Princess Royal, American abolitionists saw it as proof that Victoria, then the most powerful woman on Earth, believed in equality.

For Randle, a plaster bust of Bonetta sculpted in 1851 by Benedetto Pistrucci, the Royal Mint’s chief engraver, symbolises the story’s “duality”. Randle saw it last year after Lovejoy had tracked it down to a private family collection in his research.

“Who gets to see what their great ancestor looked like as a child, the cultural markings on her face? That is amazing. But at the same time it was a bust prepared for phrenological purposes, within a racist framework, where [Bonetta] was shown as an ‘excellent specimen’,” Randle said.

Randle first learned his family history from his father, Adekunle Randle, a retired lawyer. The family still has the engraved goblet and plate that Queen Victoria gave to Bonetta’s daughter, Victoria, who, with the queen’s help, was educated at Cheltenham ladies’ college.
Lovejoy’s book challenges the myths that Bonetta was a Yoruba princess, that she herself was Queen Victoria’s goddaughter, and that she spent most of her life in England.

Randle, 37, who maintains his family’s ancestral ties with Òkè-Òdàn, welcomes research into Bonetta, who was a gifted linguist, musician, travel writer, educator and leading woman in 19th-century Lagos, until her death from tuberculosis in Madeira in 1880, aged 37.

“Whether [Lovejoy’s] book is comfortable for me is beside the point,” Randle said. “It’s for the advancement of knowledge and how we learn from the past. Where the real discomfort lies is in what [Bonetta] was the symbol of, what she was used for.

“But it would be a mistake to paint her story as entirely tragic,” he added. “My great-great-grandmother was very capable, courageous and dignified through adversity – through the trauma of losing her family, being displaced, and changing like a chameleon to fit into a culture so alien from what she’d known, she thrived. She is an early example of Black Britain.”

articles.title: India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
articles.summary: Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

image.caption: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was released a day after his detentionImage: Dinesh Joshi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.
The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.
The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."
"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.
Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.
In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."
"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."
What are the protests about?
All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.
Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.

Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.
The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.
The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP
Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".
BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.
Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."

"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.
India: Protesters jailed amid election row
Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday
Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.
Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.
The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.
"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

articles.title: Senate eyes resolution on Chinese Embassy's dare on persona non grata call vs ambassador - Ejercito
articles.summary: The Senate is considering to issue a resolution in response to the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines' challenge to declare Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 2:24pm
The Senate is considering to issue a resolution in response to the Chinese Embassy in the Philippines' challenge to declare Ambassador Jing Quan persona non grata, Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday.

Ejercito described Jing Quan’s earlier statement as “very rude, very hostile, and very undeplomatic,” after the latter claimed that China would "easily win" if it resorted to force in the West Philippine Sea.

“Hintayin na lang natin ang plenary... Pinag-uusapan na kung magpapasa kami ng resolusyon ukol sa kanyang pananalita. Pero malamang, magkakaroon ng aksyon at resolusyon ang Senado ukol dito,” Ejercito told Super Radyo dzBB.
(Let us wait for the plenary session. We are already discussing whether to file a resolution regarding his remarks. But most likely, the Senate will take action and issue a resolution on the matter.)

On Saturday, the Chinese Embassy released a statement amid talks of possibly declaring Jung Quan persona non grata after his remarks were perceived by some lawmakers as “threats” against the Philippines.
"Some senators and house representatives are talking about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata. Is this threat or coercion?" the Chinese Embassy said in a social media post.
"But anyway, just do it. Otherwise, STOP BLUFFING," it added.
Ejercito said Jing Quan should be replaced as Chinese ambassador, saying his remarks were already threatening in nature and only adds to the tension and conflict between the two countries.

“Maganda, dapat mapalitan na lang ito. Itong Chinese ambassador belongs to a group na talagang nag-i-instigate. Parang sinasadyang talaga nila 'yan at hindi 'yan nakatutulong sa ating pag-repair o pag-ayos sa relasyon [ng Pilipinas at China],” Ejercito said.

(It would be better if he were replaced. This Chinese ambassador belongs to a group that deliberately instigates tensions. It seems they are doing this on purpose, and it does not help repair or improve relations between the Philippines and China.)
“Dapat palitan 'yan ng Tsina, kung seryoso silang ayusin ang relasyon sa ating bansa,” he added.
(China should replace him if it is serious about improving relations with our country.)
Meanwhile, Senator Jinggoy Estrada urged caution against hastily declaring someone persona non grata.

“While I share the concern and indignation his words have stirred, we must protest strongly and demand respect, without closing the doors of dialogue. Walang magandang idudulot ang padalus-dalos na pagkilos bilang tugon sa mga sinabi ng Chinese envoy (taking hasty action in response to the Chinese envoy’s remarks will do no good)," Estrada said in a statement.
“Madaling sabihin ang pagdedeklara ng persona non grata, pero ang pananagutan sa magiging kahihinatnan nito ay hindi madaling pasanin,” he added.
(Declaring someone persona non grata is easy to say, but the responsibility for its consequences is not easy to bear.)

Tensions continue as Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, a conduit for more than $3 trillion of annual shipborne commerce, including parts claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei.

The West Philippine Sea refers to the maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within, and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled in favor of the Philippines over China's claims in the South China Sea, saying that it had "no legal basis."
China has refused to recognize the decision. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: PH, US eye expanded cooperation on energy security
articles.summary: The Philippines and the United States are looking to expand their cooperation on energy security and diversify energy sources following a meeting in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 1:50pm
The Philippines and the United States are looking to expand their cooperation on energy security and diversify energy sources following a meeting in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 15.
Department of Energy (DOE) Secretary Sharon Garin met with her US counterpart, Chris Wright, to discuss potential cooperation in liquefied natural gas (LNG), coal, geothermal and nuclear energy.
“Our priority is to ensure a secure, reliable, and affordable energy supply for Filipino families and businesses," Garin said in a statement.

Strengthening our partnership with the United States will help us diversify our energy sources, develop indigenous resources, and build the technical capabilities needed to support our long-term energy security,” she added.
The two countries are also exploring potential cooperation on strategic petroleum reserves, according to the DOE.
On nuclear energy, the officials discussed cooperation under the Philippines-US Agreement for Cooperation Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy, which took effect in 2024.

“Both sides discussed initiatives supporting the Philippines' preparations for nuclear power development, including the US Department of State's Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) program, which supports technical and institutional capacity-building for safe and responsible nuclear energy development,” the DOE said.

The officials also highlighted a US Trade and Development Agency-funded reverse trade mission aimed at connecting Philippine leaders and industry stakeholders with American nuclear technology suppliers and experts in financing, regulatory affairs and workforce training.

The meeting also covered opportunities to develop indigenous energy resources, particularly geothermal energy and natural hydrogen. The officials examined Koloma's local exploration efforts and how these could contribute to the Philippines' long-term energy mix, the DOE said.
The agency said it would continue pursuing international partnerships to strengthen the country's energy supply.

The government is also promoting the Philippines as a potential oil storage hub for Asia, with the DOE proposing to allow foreign countries to establish storage facilities in the country.--MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Save-On-Foods loyalty program members had personal information accessed in cybersecurity breach
articles.summary: A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach. The chain says it discovered the activity…

image.caption: Save-On-Foods requires online shoppers to have a More Rewards profile, on top of anyone hoping to receive in-store discounts. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach. The chain says it discovered the activity on one of its servers, which was "quickly contained" before launching an investigation.
Names were accessed, possibly contact information and addresses, but no number on how many affected
A major Canadian supermarket chain has notified customers in its loyalty program that their personal information was accessed during a cybersecurity breach.

The Western Canadian grocery chain Save-On-Foods says it discovered unauthorized activity on one of its servers on Oct. 13, which was "quickly contained" before launching an investigation with a cybersecurity expert.
An email was then sent out to More Rewards customers Friday.
"We are writing to let you know about an incident involving your personal information," the email read.
Customers who received an email were told that their names and — if provided — addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and dates of birth were accessed.
CBC News asked Save-On-Foods how many customers were affected in the data breach but did not receive a number by deadline.
Save-On-Foods requires online shoppers to be signed up for the More Rewards program, which also offers members exclusive in-store discounts.
The email said "based on the information available," no other personal information, such as credit card data or passwords, was accessed.
Phishing concerns

However, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security says personal information can be used by cybercriminals to make phishing attacks more convincing, impersonating trusted organizations to trick people into sharing sensitive information or sending money.
"Most of these break-ins are opportunistic," wrote Richard Frank, director of Simon Fraser University’s international cybercrime centre, in an email to CBC News.
He said criminals often gain access to corporate networks through employees accidentally clicking malicious links or downloading malware.
But that’s when criminals can "map the network," identify whatever they can steal to monetize, "and loyalty programs usually provide enough details to make realistic scams."

Frank explained that personal information is often used by cybercriminals to impersonate companies in emails requesting more information or containing malicious links, potentially allowing them to steal identities, banking information or credit card details.
He said criminals can use that more sensitive information to make fraudulent purchases through online stores and even cryptomarkets.
Community response

Numerous Reddit commenters on B.C. and Alberta sub-communities expressed frustration with discount systems that require customers to provide personal information through loyalty programs, arguing data like that can be sold corporately and makes them a target for cybercrime.
Several of those subreddit posts suggest that customers who received the notification and then tried to change their passwords were met with a recurring error.

More Rewards members are being told to be vigilant about suspicious calls or messages, as Save-On-Foods says it will not send any communications asking for passwords, banking information, payment information, social insurance numbers or security question answers.
In an email to CBC News, Save-On-Foods said it notified the appropriate authorities and privacy regulators.
CBC News reached out to the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for B.C. to confirm whether it had been notified of the incident but did not hear back before publication.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Arden McLeod, from Vancouver, is an associate producer with CBC News. He has a passion for community storytelling, local news, and reflecting the values of B.C. He graduated from the British Columbia Institute of Technology's broadcast and online journalism program. You can reach him at Arden.McLeod@cbc.ca.

articles.title: P7M offered for 4 Maserati luxury cars during negotiated sale - BOC
articles.summary: An offer of P7,055,664 was made to four Maserati luxury cars during a recently conducted negotiated sale, the Bureau of Customs (BOC) said on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 12:58pm
An offer of P7,055,664 was made to four Maserati luxury cars during a recently conducted negotiated sale, the Bureau of Customs (BOC) said on Sunday.
Among the units auctioned were two 2021 Maserati Levante Modena with respective accepted offers of P1,594,388 and P1,601,000.
There were also two 2021 Maserati Levante GT Hybrid with accepted offers of P1,930,088 and P1,930,188, respectively.
Fast Car Traders Corp. submitted the accepted offers during the negotiated sale.
However, the sale of the vehicles is not yet final, as the agreed prices still require approval from the Department of Finance (DOF) before the transaction can be fully executed, the BOC said.

“Ang layunin natin ay matiyak na ang mga sasakyang nasa kustodiya ng BOC ay mapapakinabangan ng pamahalaan sa legal at transparent na paraan. Mahalaga na masunod ang lahat ng kinakailangang proseso at pag-apruba upang masiguro na patas ang bawat transaksyon at napoprotektahan ang interes ng taumbayan," said BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno in a statement.

(Our goal is to ensure that the vehicles in BOC custody are put to good use by the government in a legal and transparent manner. It is essential that all required processes and approvals are followed to guarantee that every transaction is fair and that the public interest is protected.)

The Department of Finance earlier said the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the BOC are expected to step up their collection efforts as the government’s total revenues are projected to reach P5.5 trillion by the end of the current administration. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: India news: Kolkata stampede dampens Durga Puja festivities
articles.summary: Authorities have detained several people over a deadly stampede in India's eastern city of Kolkata, after the state vowed strict action. Meanwhile, 'Cockroach' leader Dipke is out of detention. DW…

image.caption: The stampede took place on Saturday evening as rain spurred crowds to pour into the festive tentImage: AFP

blocks.text: October 18, 2026
Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action

blocks.caption: Relatives of the stampede's victims described confusion and darkness inside the venue before the incidentImage: AFP

blocks.text: Police in India's eastern metropolitan city of Kolkata detained 12 people on Saturday night, including the organizers of Chor Bagan Durga Puja, as they probe a stampede that killed nearly 20 people.

The latest update from the state's Chief Minister's X account puts the death toll at 17, with another 25 injured. However, Indian media, including news agency Press Trust of India (PTI), reported that at least 19 people had died.
The detentions came after West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari promised strict action against those who failed to carry out their duties to maintain crowd safety.

"We have detained 12 people in connection with our probe into the Chor Bagan incident. Our officers are talking to them to find out the cause that led to today's mishap. If any lapses are found, we will act as per the law," the officer told PTI.
Meanwhile, the West Bengal government has announced an independent investigation into the matter, led by a sitting judge of the city's high court.

"We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.
The politics of Durga Puja
Stampedes at religious and cultural festivals are not uncommon in India, but Adhikari's government is under pressure to make the city's biggest annual festival a hit this year.

blocks.caption: Several major venues housing idols of the Goddess Durga were temporarily closed on Saturday nightImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Adhikari belongs to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party which won the state elections in West Bengal for the first time in India's history, ending former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's 15-year rule there.

The festive season was facing pressure even before it began. Food and fuel inflation, worsened by the conflict in the Middle East and lower than normal rainfall at home, is eating into people's disposable incomes.

Amit Shah, India's Union Home Minister — and Modi's right-hand man — is set to visit the victims and their family members on Sunday morning. The minister had arrived in Kolkata on Saturday evening for a series of festive programs which have now been postponed.

articles.title: Network of polytechnic educators in PH launched
articles.summary: A consortium of educational institutions seeking to strengthen polytechnic education in the Philippines was recently launched during a national summit last October 14 to 16.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 12:19pm
A consortium of educational institutions seeking to strengthen polytechnic education in the Philippines was recently launched during a national summit last October 14 to 16.
The Philippine Polytechnic Education Network (PhilPEN) was launched during the National Summit on Polytechnic Education led by the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP).

“Let's work together as one polytechnic. Let us build a consortium that will advance polytechnic education, that will contribute to national progress while responding to global challenges,” said PUP president Manuel Muhi.

PhilPEN aims to establish a Philippine Polytechnic Education Framework to harmonize curricula, elevate quality assurance standards, and promote work-integrated learning for evolving workforce demands.
The network will expand cross-border applied research, strengthen industry partnerships, and address real-world community challenges.
With support from the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and alignment with ASEAN polytechnic practices, PhilPEN also seeks to enhance regional labor mobility and international collaboration.

"We gather not just to improve what we do but to redefine who we are. As polytechnic leaders, our purpose is clear: to build an education ecosystem where knowledge serves communities, research solves real problems, and our greatest measure of success is the public value we create," said PUP Vice President for Research, Extension and Development Anna Ruby Gapasin.

The summit was participated by several state universities and colleges such as the Adiong Memorial State College, Camarines Sur Polytechnics Colleges, Dalubhasaang Politekniko ng Lungsod ng Baliwag, Ilocos Sur Polytechnic State College, Laguna State Polytechnic University, Limay Polytechnic College, Marikina Polytechnic College, Navotas Polytechnic College, Pangasinan Polytechnic College, Polytechnic College of Botolan, Palompon Institute of Technology, and Eulogio Amang Rodriguez Institute of Science and Technology.

Representatives from the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority and the Technical Vocational Schools Association also participated in the three-day summit. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
articles.summary:
Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and…
articles.byline: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands; photographs and video by Sean Smith

blocks.text: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors, of varying popularity, gazed disinterestedly at the scene.

blocks.caption: The Falkland Islands, home to approximately 3,600 residents

blocks.text: Proceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.

It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.
“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.
But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.

“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.

blocks.caption: Assembly members Roger Spink, Stacy Bragger and Lewis Clifton before the monthly meeting.

blocks.text: Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.

“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”

Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.

The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.

blocks.caption: Aerial view of a new port and floating jetty being built in the Falkland Islands.

blocks.text: In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpol received Foreign Office representations suggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.

For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.

“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.

blocks.caption: Ricky Evans, who runs a guesthouse and other businesses, carries post and supplies for Stanley.

blocks.text: The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.

Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.

There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.

blocks.caption: Chilean tourists pose for a photograph outside the Stanley post office.

blocks.text: Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”

Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.

blocks.caption: John Barton, chair of the Falkland Islands fishing companies association and James Bates, the executive secretary.

blocks.text: All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.

In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.

The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.

blocks.caption: James Wallace, who runs the Fortuna fishing company, onboard his harbour launch.
A worker packs filleted toothfish into plastic bags at a Falkland Islands processing factory.

blocks.text: James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.

The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.

blocks.caption: A bust of Margaret Thatcher by the 1982 war memorial.

blocks.text: About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.

Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.

blocks.caption: Chief executive of the Falklands government, Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.

blocks.text: Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.

Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.

Clausen sees trauma throughout the islands. “I guess, some extreme behaviour,” she said. “Anger, aggression on certain political subjects.” She is evidently frustrated by the recent Argentinian actions.
“The Falklands has since [19]82 ensured that we are financially independent – save for defence,” she said. “We had no money in 82 and we never want to be in that position again.”

The oil is their insurance, she suggested. “I like to think that better people will de-escalate this because, honestly, we are 4,000 people minding our own business, we have a history deeper and older than theirs.”

blocks.caption: Falkland Islands reserves (from left): Cpl Chris Stenning; Justin McPhee, director of emergency services; Lt Alastair Baylis; and warrant officer second class Paul Watson.

blocks.text: There are cycles to Argentinian bellicosity. The opportunistic but ill-fated invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator general Leopoldo Galtieri, leading to the death of 649 Argentinians and 255 British military personnel, along with three islanders, has cast a pall over Argentinian-UK relations ever since.

But at times, notably in the 1990s, Buenos Aires adopted a hearts-and-minds approach to the islanders, sending videos of the animated series Pingu to their children. Such kindness has tended to evaporate away, though, when an Argentinian government is losing public support at home, as Milei is experiencing now.

But if any one attribute sums up the islanders, it is resilience, said Dot Gould, an assembly member who owns Pebble, a 20-mile long island north-west of the Falklands. She and her husband share the island with a couple who run a lodge, 5,000 sheep, 100 cattle, a load of spectacular wildlife, but not much else.

blocks.caption: Dot Gould, who owns Pebble island.

blocks.text: Rampaging around the undulating terrain in her 4x4 vehicle, avoiding colonies of Rockhopper and Gentoo penguins, Gould points out the scattered remains of an Argentinian fighter jet and the graves of two of the airmen killed during battle. As a child on Pebble, she used to play with the parachutes left by the Argentinians, using them as sails for a go-kart.

“I think, since 1982, this is probably the most serious it’s been for us,” she said. “How effective they will be, we don’t know yet … it’s almost two fingers up: we’ll get on with it, we have to.” But there is much that they want to do.

The islands are dependent on a narrow range of freight links from the UK and South America for much of their fresh produce. Any glitch, and peculiar shortages can emerge. There was a period without milk. A time without beer. During one cherry tomato shortage, which saw their price shoot up, the main supermarket opted to cut them in half and sell them like that to spread the joy.

A sorry-looking cabbage will set you back £8 at the West Store on the front. The local newspaper is the Penguin News (“This one’s not for Penguin News but …” is the traditional opening when disseminating islands gossip). But Facebook is the key means of communication. “Grown men and women use Snapchat like teenagers, often to arrange their extramarital affairs,” said one local.

blocks.caption: Children during school lunch break.

blocks.text: Other peculiarities include the Falklands government paying for children from the age of 16 to complete their secondary and university education in the UK. The size of the islands’ population makes it impractical to offer such levels of education at home, said Sarah Stannard, the islands’ director of education.

But if the oil money comes online, she would rebuild the primary school. Children from the countryside – it is known locally as “camp” – are offered board in Stanley, although there are also peripatetic teachers and lessons done on the telephone.

The children grow up quickly here, and tend to be keen to broaden their horizons. Oliver Lee, 15, was keen to join the merchant navy. “I would like to see other places,” he said. “The Mediterranean, hotter places basically.” Layla-May Vatemanu, 14, said: “A lot of the boys especially in my class do a lot of sport. Our [friendship group] doesn’t have a lot to do.”

blocks.caption: School students (from left): Oliver Lee, Layla May, Tessa Blake and Paul Green.

blocks.text: There are no bus services anywhere, and the more distant parts of the islands are only accessible via boat or the Falkland government’s twin-engine aircraft service. On a landmass half the size of Wales, there is only one cashpoint.

Touch rugby – rather than full-contact rugby – is played, in part because the islands’ hospital does not have the capability to deal with complex injuries. Much of the health budget goes on medi-evacs to South America. Yet, for all that, most of the children who leave at 16 do return.

All places are shaped by their history and geography, but some have more history and geography than others. “We are British with a twist,” said Stacy Bragger, a former journalist who represents the Stanley constituency in the assembly.

“We have our own identity. If you were to ask what are the traits of a Falkland islander – resourcefulness, resilience, making do. Because if something breaks you can’t just go down the road. You have to make do. That’s our version of Britishness.”

blocks.caption: Mike Summers (left) and Liam Short, members of the chamber of commerce.

blocks.text: The islanders also have long memories. “I used to read the Guardian when I was a good deal younger,” said Mike Summers, 73, who sits on the board of the local chamber of commerce. “But I stopped reading it in 1982 when [the editor] Peter Preston just fucked me off so much. He was: ‘Oh well they are a long way away and there is only a few of them – so why don’t we just sell them?’”

On the Argentinian rhetoric, Summers added: “There are a lot of people who still suffer effects from the war – PTSD among the older people. I bumped into someone at the supermarket the other day who I have known for ever. She said: ‘Oh, I’m wondering if I should sell my house and move away. The Argies are going to invade again.’ It seriously affects some people and it is cruel actually.”

blocks.caption: Social influencer Roxy King-Clark at her home in Stanley.

blocks.text: Roxy King-Clarke, 40, describes herself as the Falklands’ biggest influencer, with about 60,000 followers. She picked up a major following when posting in response to the Argentinian men’s football team brandishing a “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” [The Malvinas are Argentinian] banner at the World Cup.

She is regularly subjected to abuse for her posts. “The most common insults are to call us pirates, usurpers and colonisers,” she said. “It’s a bizarre thing to be on the receiving end of it all as they speak like we’ve just tipped up here. I can trace my family back to my earliest ancestor arriving here in 1842.”

Her generation too, she suggests, have taken lessons from what happened four decades ago. King-Clarke said she would take a “hard line” to avoid any misinterpretation. “We need to learn from history,” she said, “and not make the same mistakes.”

articles.title: ‘Serious incident’ at Alberta military base causes deaths and injuries, Canada officials say
articles.summary:
Incident at CFB Wainwright base in Alberta caused a ‘major fire’ that is spreading to the nearby town because of strong winds

People have been killed and injured after an incident at one of…

blocks.text: People have been killed and injured after an incident at one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta caused a large fire, Canada’s defence minister said Saturday.
“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” defence minister David McGuinty said at a press conference on Saturday night.

McGuinty described the situation at CFB Wainwright as “active and delicate” with the fire being monitored very closely. “I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory”, he said at the press conference.

McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support.
In an earlier social media post, prime minister Mark Carney said: “A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.”
“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said.

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base’s fence earlier Saturday and was spreading rapidly due to high winds. Firefighters from multiple jurisdictions were responding, and no evacuation order was in effect.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, about 180km southeast of Edmonton, is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
Neither Carney nor Smith provided details about what caused the fire or whether anyone was injured.

articles.title: DOH warns of harmful effects of cadmium found in vape
articles.summary: DOH warns of harmful effects of cadmium found in vape

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 10:35am
The Department of Health (DOH) on Sunday warned the public about the harmful health effects of cadmium, a toxic metal found in vape aerosols.
Cadmium can damage the kidneys and bones, while prolonged exposure may increase the risk of cancer, the DOH said in Mao dela Cruz’s Super Radyo dzBB report.
.@DOHgovph, nagbabala laban sa masamang epekto sa kalusugan ng cadmium, na natatagpuan sa aerosol ng vape. | via Mao Dela Cruz https://t.co/q15027pz56— DZBB Super Radyo (@dzbb) October 18, 2026
Aside from cadmium, vape aerosols may contain other harmful chemicals, including benzene, diacetyl, and acrolein.
The DOH urged the public, particularly the youth, to avoid vaping due to its harmful components.
It also backed calls to implement higher taxes on vapes to help make potentially harmful products less affordable and accessible.
Earlier this month, the Philippine Tobacco Harm Reduction Advocates (PHILTRA) said health advocates urged the government to consider higher excise taxes on vape products.
E-liquids are currently taxed differently depending on whether they contain salt nicotine or freebase nicotine.

Meanwhile, the Department of Finance is proposing a unified excise tax of P72.93 per 2 milliliters or 2 grams on e-cigarettes and heated tobacco products, on top of a P150 excise tax per device. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Over 1,000 special permits issued to PUVs for Undas 2026
articles.summary: More than 1,000 special permits have been issued to several public utility vehicles (PUVs) amid the expected influx of passengers this Undas break, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory…

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 10:10am

More than 1,000 special permits have been issued to several public utility vehicles (PUVs) amid the expected influx of passengers this Undas break, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said on Sunday.
"Marami na po. In fact, nasa around 1,200 to 1,300 there about po na na-issue na special permits, units na po 'yun," said LTFRB acting chairperson Greg Pua, Jr. in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(There are already many. In fact, around 1,200 to 1,300 special permits have been issued to individual units.)
The LTFRB said the special permits were issued to buses, mini buses and passenger vans.
"May mga bus, mini bus, may mga van din po," said Pua.
(There are buses, mini-buses, and also vans.)
While there were more special permits issued this year, the LTFRB is expecting more units to apply.

"I heard po yung mga samahan ng mga provincial buses, inup na po nila yung kanilang mga advanced bookings at online bookings, so malalaman na po nila kung kulang pa po yung kanilang mga buses. We expect pa po until next week, siguro, marami pang applications na masa-submit," said Pua.

(I heard the provincial bus groups have already opened their advance and online bookings, so they will be able to determine if they still lack buses. We still expect more applications to be submitted, probably until next week.)
The agency said there will LTFRB desks in some bus stations to accommodate more special permit applications.
"Nandoon po kami sa mga terminal para kung sakaling mayroon po yung mga kulang pa, makapag-issue kami agad," said Pua.
(We will be stationed at the terminals so that if there are still shortages, we can issue permits immediately.)
The All Saints' Day will fall on Sunday, November 1, while the All Souls' Day will be on Monday, November 2. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Canada: Fire at Alberta military Base kills four, leaves 19 in critical condition
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at on Alberta military base. Four people have died, 39 are in hospital and at least 19 are in critical condition.

image.caption: Officials have warned of 'overwhelmed' hospitals Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an update on Sunday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were in hospital after a fire at a Canadian military base that killed four people. At least 19 were in critical condition.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday called the incident one of the worst tragedies the army has suffered in peace time.

"It is with deep sadness that I can confirm, at this time, that four service members have lost their lives and that their loved ones have been notified," Carney said in the capital Ottawa, adding that "dozens of others have been seriously injured."
"We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery," Carney said.
"And we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss, they will not carry it alone because in Canada we take care of one another."
Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper reported on Sunday that a smoldering grass fire was whipped into a wall of flames by high winds.
The fire then engulfed Canadian Armed Forces members at a firing range, the newspaper said, citing internal military communications.
Medical facilities around base 'overwhelmed'

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, which is located some 180 kilometers (120 miles) northwest of the base, told national broadcaster CBC that people were being brought to hospitals across the city.

Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, said health-care facilities around the base itself had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people requiring medical aid.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," he said. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

blocks.caption: The injured were brought to Wainwright Health CenterImage: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?
The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds.
"The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected.
"We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

articles.title: B.C. municipal elections: Polls close in less than an hour as voters choose next mayors, councillors

blocks.text: B.C. Votes: Municipal elections 2026

Voters in 161 B.C. municipalities go to the polls to elect their next mayor and council, school board and, in some cases, park board. Join hosts Lien Yeung and Stephen Quinn along with Jason D'Souza, Chris Walker and Justin McElroy for live coverage and analysis as results come in from from across the province.
The Latest

items: Millions of British Columbians are choosing their next local governments today, with voting open in municipalities across the province.
More than 3,500 candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., including municipalities and regional districts.
Heading into election day, local leaders were worried about confusion and low turnout given the provincial election takes place a week from today.
Polls close provincewide at 8 p.m. local time.

October 18Surrey candidates weigh new facilities and housing growthAkshay KulkarniSurrey mayor says $360M Vancouver Giants arena will be built on timeThe City of Surrey plans to build a 10,000-seat hockey arena that will be the new home of the WHL's Vancouver Giants. Surrey Mayor Brenda Locke defended the project, and said it would not lead to unnecessary costs for taxpayers while Giants majority owner Ron Toigo says the team will not immediately move to rename itself the Surrey Giants.Surrey's mayoral candidates have promised a range of new community and recreation facilities if elected, including a waterfront district, a conference centre and new pools.Building community infrastructure to serve Surrey's burgeoning population has been a big issue for years, with a 10,000-seat arena the latest major facility to be greenlit — even as the cost of the police transition weighs on the city's budget.The major candidates, however, have different ideas on how they'll balance housing and population growth to go along with those large projects.Locke says she will build on her work in the past, including approving more than 13,800 net new units.Annis and McCallum, meanwhile, are pushing back on the province's push for more dense housing centred around public transit. Annis says infrastructure needs to keep up with growth, while McCallum is pushing for the Crescent Beach and Ocean Park areas to be excluded from provincial housing legislation.Starchuk has promised to build more affordable homes on city land, with priority for family-sized homes.Troy Van Vliet is promising a family housing policy to include targets for two- and three-bedroom homes, while Honveer Randhawa says he would guarantee that building permits for single-family homes and renovations stamped by authorized firms are issued within five business days.

Race to watch: Locke and McCallum face off again in SurreyAkshay KulkarniWho will be the next mayor of Surrey?CBC’s The Early Edition brought together five candidates vying to be mayor of Surrey for two debates: Mike Starchuk with Imagine Surrey, Surrey city councillor Linda Annis, incumbent mayor Brenda Locke, Conservative Party of Surrey candidate Honveer Randhawa and Troy Van Vilet, a Surrey builder and business owner.Much like in Vancouver, former council allies are competing for the mayoral role in Surrey, B.C.'s second-largest city by population and one whose population growth rate led Canada for many years.Incumbent Brenda Locke of Surrey Connect was formerly a councillor under Doug McCallum, the city's mayor between 2018 and 2022 who is now running again with the Safe Surrey Coalition.The pair split in 2019 over McCallum's support for an independent Surrey Police Service (SPS), with Locke preferring to stay with the Surrey RCMP.With that issue now largely in the rearview mirror — the province having ordered the transition to the SPS — Locke and McCallum join a crowded field as they aim for the city's top job once again.Among those on the list are Coun. Linda Annis, who leads the Surrey First slate, and former MLA and councillor Mike Starchuk, leader of the Imagine Surrey slate.Two candidates — Honveer Randhawa of the Conservative Electors Association and Troy Van Vliet of Surrey Now — haven't held elected office before.

Property taxes a key issue in VancouverAkshay KulkarniVancouver Mayor Ken Sim promises tax freeze and community centres if re-electedVancouver Mayor Ken Sim made his final State of the City address for his first term to the Board of Trade on Wednesday, and with it came two big election promises. Justin McElroy reports on what the mayor is putting front and centre in his platform. Sim swept to power with a super-majority in 2022 on the back of a campaign largely focused on public safety.After four years as mayor, Sim is now promising a property tax freeze if an ABC majority is elected, after the 2026 budget featured one, too.All the other major candidates in the race have slammed that move and Sim's promise, with Fry saying the budgeted property tax freeze led to major cutbacks in city services and administration. Fry has promised more accessible, line-item budgets if he's elected.Allam has promised to cap property tax increases to the rate of inflation, while Hardwick is also promising "predictable increases" in line with inflation.Bligh has promised to replace the property tax freeze with increases based on long-term planning.

Race to watch: Vancouver mayoral race features 5 main slatesAkshay KulkarniVancouver’s mayoral field shifts into focusAfter a week where two Vancouver mayoral candidates left the race, voters are getting a clearer sense of the main choices on the ballot next month. As the CBC's Justin McElroy reports, they’re all trying to position themselves in slightly different ways.The leaders of five major political slates are aiming to be mayor of B.C.'s most populous city.They include the incumbent, Ken Sim of ABC Vancouver, and his former chief of staff, Kareem Allam, who is running for the Vancouver Liberals.Two longtime councillors — Pete Fry of the Vancouver Greens, and Rebecca Bligh of Vote Vancouver — are also in the race, as is former councillor Colleen Hardwick of TEAM Vancouver.Bligh was kicked out of ABC Vancouver last year while Hardwick ran for council in 2018 with Sim, who was then the NPA's mayoral candidate.Fry was the only opposition voice in the previous council for a period of time due to councillor vacancies and an ABC super-majority.

What does a local government do?Arden McLeodWhat municipalities can and can’t do in B.C.With municipal and provincial elections going on at the same time, it can be hard to know which promises being made at the local level are realistic, and which ones aren’t. The CBC’s Justin McElroy explains what powers cities actually have.Many major funding and policy decisions sit with the province and its ministries. But Kimberly Speers, who teaches public administration at UVic, says people can feel the impact of local government decisions every day."It's not generally seen as, you know, an exciting part of governing ... but at the same time, my gosh, are those local services so, so important," Speers said.Municipalities like Vancouver tend to spend the most on protective services, such as police, fire, and emergency services.Another big ticket item for municipalities is utilities like water, sewage and waste. Municipalities also oversee parks, recreation and culture centres and how land-use is determined — as well as maintaining sidewalks, roads and public transportation.

Multiple votes to cast in civic electionsArden McLeodElection overload is real in B.C. ahead of 2 back-to-back votesElection overload is real in B.C. with 2 back-to-back votesMunicipal political parties generally don't map neatly onto provincial parties across B.C., and depending on where you live, polling can include elections for bodies like school boards, as well as for mayor and council.In Vancouver, for instance, residents are voting for one mayor, 10 city councillors, seven park board commissioners and nine school board trustees.In provincial elections, on the other hand, voters simply choose one candidate to represent their riding in the legislature.

Record number of advance voters in some municipalitiesAkshay KulkarniA cyclist heading toward an advance voting station in Vancouver. (Nav Rahi/CBC)Vancouver is among many municipalities that saw a record number of residents make use of advance voting opportunities for this election.The city says 103,000 voters cast a ballot over four advance voting days, smashing a record of 65,127 in 2022. Officials also say mail-in voting requests doubled compared to 2022, with 21,000 requests this year.Surrey and Kelowna, among others, also saw high advance voter turnouts.Every municipality was required to provide at least one advance voting day in B.C.That's encouraging because, despite a local government's major impact on voters' lives — given they are usually responsible for day-to-day services like garbage collection, sewage and policing — voter turnout in B.C.'s civic elections are usually lower than provincial and federal elections.In 2022, 29.2 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot, well below the turnout for the subsequent provincial and federal elections, according to CivicInfoBC.

It's election night in British Columbia – the 1st of 2Rhianna SchmunkA voting sign in Vancouver on Oct. 7. (Nav Rahi/CBC)British Columbians are choosing their next local representatives on councils, school boards and other regional posts on Saturday, the first of two election days this month.The Union of B.C. Municipalities says more than 3,500 local government candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., which include municipalities and regional districts. CBC's Decision Desk will be closely following the vote count after polls close across most of the province at 8 p.m. local time, and will deliver projections of the results in some of B.C.'s biggest communities, including Kamloops, Kelowna, Richmond, Surrey, Vancouver and Victoria.The overlapping provincial election had many worried about widespread voter confusion. Still, many cities and municipalities reported increased or even record turnout at advance polls, including Vancouver, Richmond, Burnaby, Kamloops, Surrey, Kelowna, Prince George, Cranbrook and View Royal.Voters will cast their ballots again next Saturday for the provincial election.

articles.title: ‘We will remember’: Tributes pour in for soldiers killed in fiery incident at Alberta military base

image.caption: Aidan Goulding. Submitted by Wylder Goulding (Submitted by Wylder Goulding)

blocks.text: The mother of one of the men killed in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base says her son was a bright light who wanted to serve his country.

Pte. Aidan Goulding, from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died Saturday after a grass fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, killing four soldiers and leaving dozens more grievously injured.

items: 4 dead, at least 19 in critical condition after deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta

blocks.text: Goulding's mother, Sonia Monk, told CBC News she knew exactly where her son was when she heard that a fire had broken out at the base.
“Aidan always told us where he was going, always told us that he loved us,” she said Sunday.
Monk said she learned that her son had died late Saturday night. Officers came to her door in British Columbia around 11 p.m.
At the sound of the bell, she said she and her husband knew instantly that something horrible had happened.
Monk said she had been trying desperately to reach her son all throughout the afternoon and evening but got no response.
“And I just kept hoping,” she said. “But they showed up at the door.”
'The light of my life'
Monk described her son as an exceptional athlete, a natural leader and a passionate young man who always accomplished his goals.
She said Goulding, 23, had only joined the military in February of this year.
He previously worked as a mechanic and loved the work because he was passionate about cars, she said, adding he only recently realized he had a different calling.

Goulding told his family that he wanted to serve his country. He enlisted, completed his basic training and quickly felt at home in the military, Monk said. His goal was to work for the military's special operations and then move on to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.
“He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up,” she said. “He really was the light of my life.
“And he really, really loved his new family.”
At a news conference in Edmonton on Sunday, officials confirmed there were many people who had been taking part in the training exercise that were badly burned.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 of the patients remained in hospital and at least 19 among them were in critical condition.
The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking, Smith said.
“To the families who lost loved ones, an entire province and millions of Canadians nationwide grieve with you,” she said.

“To our injured and to our military community, and to the people of Wainwright, Alberta stands shoulder to shoulder with you, and not just today in the immediate aftermath, but every step of the way along the road to recovery.
“In the days ahead, our thoughts remain with everyone affected by this tragedy.”

items: Flags flying at half mast in Manitoba after deadly fire at Alberta military base

blocks.text: The cause of the fire and reports that the flames set off a series of blasts, remain under investigation.
All four of the dead were based in Alberta but hailed from communities across Western Canada. Their names were revealed for the first time Sunday.
Sgt. Morgan Wong, from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (PPCLI), hailed from Edmonton.
Pte. Shaun Farrell, from 3rd Battalion PPCLI, was from Prince Albert, Sask. Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, from 3rd Battalion PPCLI, was from Langley, B.C. Goulding was originally from North Vancouver.
In a post on social media Sunday, 49th Battalion, Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said its members were deeply saddened by the loss of Wong and all others who lost their lives.

“On behalf of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association, we extend our heartfelt condolences to their families, friends, and fellow soldiers. Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this tragedy.
“We will remember them.”

items: CFB Wainwright fire started during multiple training exercises

blocks.text: In a statement Sunday, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe offered his condolences to the victims and their families, particularly Farrell, a Saskatchewan soldier. He also thanked first responders, medical teams and emergency crews who continue to support those affected.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the Canadian Armed Forces, the Wainwright community, and families across Canada," Moe wrote.
"Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him.
“As we remember Shaun and the other service members who lost their lives, we also keep those injured and their loved ones in our thoughts.”
Shaun Farrell of Saskatchewan was among four soldiers killed after a fire swept across CFB Wainwright Saturday afternoon. (Patricia Farrell/Facebook)

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, inaugural commander of the revitalized 1st Canadian Division, told reporters that the fire that sparked Saturday afternoon moved rapidly across the prairie landscape amid fierce and shifting winds, catching troops at CFB Wainwright by surprise on the field.
Rutland said the grass fire was initially burning about a kilometre away from Canadian Armed Forces members during training exercises.
'A fire right on top of them'

Range control officials managing the training exercise were aware of the fire for hours but ruled that it was sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to continue, Rutland said.
But the winds suddenly and violently shifted, he said, pushing the fire in towards service members. Within seconds, the flames descended upon the soldiers.
"I spoke to my commander on the ground," Rutland explained. "He said, within 30 seconds to a minute, they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them."

What happened next remains under investigation, Rutland said. He explained that the training exercise taking place involved live munitions. On one range, soldiers were throwing hand grenades, while on another range soldiers were conducting what the military calls a section attack.
Rutland said the strength of the fire seen on the landscape could have been made worse by a number of munitions and weapons involved in the training exercises.
“There was a multitude of ordinances moving through the Wainwright training area,” he said.
“Grenade launchers, grenades, small arms, ammunition — quite frankly, it could have been any of that or none of it.”

Rutland said there will be a thorough investigation of the circumstances surrounding the tragedy, what caused the flames to spread, how the fire moved unseen across the landscape and if the base responded appropriately to the threat posed by the grass fire.
CFB Wainwright fire started during multiple training exercises

The wounded are being cared for at hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer. Due to the severity of their injuries, provincial health officials have said many of those injured face a long and difficult recovery.

National Defence Minister David McGuinty spoke at the same news conference with Smith and Rutland Sunday. He said the soldiers and reservists involved in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright are from across the country.
"This loss reaches communities in every province," he said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the deadly fire one of the worst tragedies for the Canadian Armed Forces on Canadian soil in peacetime.

articles.title: Sara Duterte can file charges vs witnesses in impeachment trial, says law professor
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte can file charges against the witnesses in her trial following the withdrawal of three articles of impeachment against her, a law professor said on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 18, 2026 8:53am
Vice President Sara Duterte can file charges against the witnesses in her trial following the withdrawal of three articles of impeachment against her, a law professor said on Sunday.

"Kung gusto ng Bise Presidente na i-vindicate ang kanyang sarili, maghain siya ng karampatang kaso sa mga tumestigo laban sa kanya, ito man perjury or violation ng confidentiality," said Adonis Gabriel of San Beda University College of Law in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(If the Vice President wants to vindicate herself, she should file the appropriate charges against those who testified against her, whether it is perjury or violation of confidentiality.)
The Senate impeachment court earlier accepted the move by the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte.

The prosecution said that it will no longer pursue three other charges against Duterte, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business.
The Vice President can also charge the senator-judges if she wishes to, said Gabriel.
"Pwede maghain ng administrative case sa Senado mismo para tignan kung mayroong paglabag sa karapatan ng depensa ang mga huwes," he added.
(An administrative case can be filed right in the Senate to check if the judges violated the rights of the defense.)

Following the withdrawal of the three articles against her, Duterte's camp said the prosecution's withdrawal of three articles of impeachment on Tuesday is an admission that the allegations hurled against her lacked basis from the start.
"The withdrawal is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning," said lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: 'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections
articles.summary: Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control…

image.caption: It was the fourth 'No Kings' protest since President Trump returned to officeImage: Madison Swart/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters gathered across the United States for the latest "No Kings" demonstrations as Americans begin casting ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," Saturday's event aimed to fire up Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, rather than protest against President Donald Trump and his administration.

"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.
Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

blocks.caption: There were more than 3,000 'No Kings' events planned across the USImage: Daniel Heuer/REUTERS

blocks.text: Trump opposes mail-in voting

Trump repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought to restrict the practice ahead of the midterms. He regularly votes by mail-in ballot, arguing that his job makes him an exception to his criticism of the practice.
The US president blamed election fraud, without providing evidence, for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election against Democrat Joe Biden.
Various surveys have concluded that restricting mail-in ballots could benefit Republicans, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.
